There are great possibilities Auresqueness, especially among brunettes, in grey Grey is the colour they 'should select, and chinchilla is their far while a touch of palest pink affords the necessary relief, warmth, and brightness. Many society women, still quite young, have perfectly grey hair, but sensibly they take no measures to colour or cover it. Countess Fritz Hochberg, a bride of last I year, has parfectly grey hair, so also has the youngand charming Lady Henry Bentinct. . Lady de Grey's hair is white, so igain is Mrs. Hall Walker's, one of the smartest of one young married women. div.head: DON'T NEGLECT YOUR SKIN.
div.p: DON'T NEGLECT YOUR SKIN.
Homely Hints for the Autumn.

All those who have to complain just now of a nasty raw" feel "about their hands, arms, necks or faces, not to mention the serious skin disease aftlictin body and limb in the autumn, would do well to realise how much of this suffering is due to neglect, and by what simple means the worst skin may be regenerated in the clear- ness and flexibility of htvalth.

Don't forget that the skin is more than a mere cover- ing to protect the body. By means of tiny pores it helps to purify the system; and a poisoned cut, an inflamed chap, or an itching sore may mean grave inter- ference with the functions so closely connected with the general health. Don't forget that the skin surfaces are being continu- ally worn away and renewed from below by the growth of new tissue. Don't forget that the damp, raw, cold days of October make the skin harden and crack, and sow the first seeds of skin disease. Cheap soaps do the same by stealing out of the pores the natural oil that should keep the skin soft and nice. •

Don't neglect a cut or a sore for fear of blood. poisoning or inflammation. Zam-buk is the best, in fact the only certain, antiseptic healer. Whether the trouble is a rash from a sudden chill, swelling and inflammation from" chaps " on washing-day, or chafing or cold-sores produced by friction or exposure—in any of these emergencies Zam-buk proves a veritable boon. l'his popular balm derives its unique properties from certain rich healing vegetable juices, and the remark- able manner of their combination.

Zam-buk works hand in hand with Nature, as befits its natural origin. It first expels all that is retarding the everyday functions of the skin. Having done this. and stimulated all the natural functions to normal activity, Zam-buk helps to replace the injured or diseased parts by thoroughly spund and healthy tissue. This marvellous work of regeneration is so minute and complicated that a powerful microscope would be required to watch the building up of a new tissue. The process may be likened to a builder extending a new row of houses. New cells are created until the whole of the injured, irritated, or diseased surface is changed. * * * *

What the sufferer first notices, as the applications of Zam-buk ars continued, is that all itching and inflam- mation are quickly allayed. The smart is taken out of the cut, burn, or scald, or in the case of disease, burning sores cease to torture, ulcers and eruptions dry up and grow less, and in the end, thanks to Zam-buk's ideal method, all disfigurement is for ever banished. No skin looks so well, or is, in fact, so soft, sound, sweet, and healthy throughout, as the skin that has had frequent dre,sings of Zam-buk. This perfection is more than -" skin-deep," seeing that a healthy skin (made healthy by Zam-bnk) often exerts a wholesome influence upon the rest of the body. * * * *

Zam-buk, because of its unique composit:on and its splendid achievements, can reasonably claim to have revived one of the lost arts of Ancient Greece. No home should be without a one-and-three-halfpenny or two-and-nine box (the latter containing nearly three times the ordinary box). Of all chemists, or from the Zam-buk co., Redcross-street, London, B.C.

div.head: ST. HELENS BUTCHER'S FAILURE.
div.p: ST. HELENS BUTCHER'S FAILURE.
Bar;nas

Creditors of Joseph Unsworth, retail butcher,' of Beech House, Prescot-road, St. Helens, who carried on business at It, Bridge-street, St. Helens, and dp rmerly at Imperial-buildings, Ormskirk-street, St. Hilrens, met on Wednesday at the offices of the Official Receiver at Liverpool. The debtor, against whom a receiving order order and an order of adjudication were made on Sep- tember 10th,presented a statement showing gross liabili- ties of £1,473, of which amount £1,161 was expected to rank for dividend. The assets consisted mainly of stock, fixtures, &c., and book debts, and the deficiency was put at £BB9. In 1897 the debtor borrowed £5OO at 5 per cent. and purchased for £368 the business in Ormskirk-street, but four years ago he fell ' behind in his payments, and two years later, the land- lord threatening an increase of rent, he took the Bridge-street shop. He ascribed his failure to bad trade and want of capital. The principal creditor was the lender of The £5OO in 1897; whose debt, with interest, is now £528, against which is held as security a mort- gage valued at £6o.—The Official Receiver, reported that the stock, fixtures, pony and trap, &c. had been sold for £6O, and of the 51298 book debts £lOO had been collected and another £5O was expected. The debtoris now in the employ of the purchaser of his business stock, but he had no offer to make to his creditors.— The public examination is fixed for October gth.

MY DEAR CHILDREN, I hope .you have all read the aanounce- ment regarding the competitions that appeared in the paper the week before last. I hope you will all make some little article for "Uncle Ned," and remember the last day for receiving these is October 15th for the girls, and the Bth inst. for the boys... •

We have several new members to welcome this week, and I am sure they are very welcome., These members have all sent me contributions, so I must give them to understand that these must wait their turn, and they may not appear for a week or two. Some of you ask me for rules. The principal ones are that all must promise to obey their parents and teachers; also any contributions that are sent must be written in ink, otherwise no prize can be awarded, and I like my members to join all the competitions that are arranged. I give away two prizes every week, and special ones for our monthly competition. All my prizes are well worth trying to gain._ _

I think that very shortly I shall ask you all to make some article of needlework for the poor this winter. Prizes will be awarded to the best made article, but I will give you full particulars in a week or so.
The prizes this' week go to Annie Howarth and Albert Capewell. •
With all good wishes rf rOm
UNCLE NED.
Dear Uncle Ned,—l have tong read the stories in the "Children's Corner," and I wish to become a member. I am sending you a story called
DEATH'S TIMEPIECE,
(Concluded from last week.)

When they left me I could not move a limb and my head was kept still by that horrible steel cap. I looked at the time; it was ten minutes past four, and already the point had started on its way. Hours, which seemed like years to me, paseed by, and at seven o'clock the point was about two feet from my mouth, still coming on so slowly yet so surely. The horror and awful feeling I went through in those 4ong hours baffles all description. That point, with ite deathly meaning, always coming on, never stopping. I became light headed, and screamed for it to go back, but the giggles out- side only increased to laughter. At eight o'clock it touched my lips, and I shuddered and screamed; but only a giggle 'came from outside. That fearful point was still coming. I opened my mouth and let the point in till at last it touched the back of my gullet. Then every- thng seemed to swim before me, and I fainted. As I did so, I,thought I heard a crash, and a bell rang, and A knew no more. When I awoke it was half-pat nine,. and I was still in the chair. \At my feet was the longest part of the bar, while a piece still show&l through the dial. Outside there was a hum of several voices and some one was banging at the door. Whit( did it mean? Why wasn't I dead? S - - the door' burst 'open, and there stood spector and twenty police. The next day I had somewhat got over my hor- rible adventure, but I was not satisfied as to how I was saved. So having seen the police inspector and told him my tale, be told me the following:—
iuddenly the i"
'lie in

The man whom we ,caught in your room we coaxed and got him to betray his league, and he told'us that they had told him that they would kill him if he would not no as he was bidden. They also told him that if he did not return safe in a quarter of an hour they would know that you had betrayed kim, and they would find some way to have vengeance. So we at once went ,to the place, and caught all of them, and saved, you, but Eta to the broken bar we know nothing about it. The wounded leader is in there, ask him. This brought the solution to my mind. When I sprang on the leader and brought the bar down, that must have broken it and when it came out to the broken part it fell off. Be that as it may, I know that now I have married the girl I was to murder, and I am the only existing one of the "Secret of Secrets."
rITZROY LOVELL.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l thought I would send you a story, which I hope you will like. It is called:

OUR BABY SISTER. She came with the summer flowers, When the world was bright and gay, And our hearts were filled with gladness On that happy summer day. There was never a baby like her, With her beautiful, bright, blue eyes, That looked in our happy faces With serious, mute surprise.
We crept on tip-toes to see her,! Jem and Bobbie and I, And we smiled as we told each other She will play with us by and by. For we had had no sister

Till this little baby came, And mother said her brown-haired boys Should choose our darling's name. So we sat round the pink-lined cradle, And talk:td quite seriously; And we „thought that " Lily " should be the best, For she was so fair, you see. But when the winter snowflakes Blew over the bleak hill-side, Our little baby sister, Our Lily drooped and died. But mother says we must not cry, For she is robed in white, And walks among the angels In a place of rest and light. And mother says our baby Was only to us given, That she might be the golden cord To draw us all to Heaven. , ANNIE HOWARTH.
Dear Uncle Ned,—l should very much like to join the "Children's Corner," and I am sending you a piece of poetry, which is called:
DRIVE THE NAIL.
Drive the nail aright, •boya, • Hit it on the head; Strike with all your might, boys, Ere the time has fled.
Lessons you've to learn, boys, Study with a will; - They who reach the top, boys, First must climb the hill.
Standing at the foot, boys, Gazing at the sky, How can you get up, boys, If you never try?
Try and try again, boys, You will win at last I Ever persevere; boys, Though youto task is hard;
Toil and happy trust, boys, Bring their own reward. Never give it up, boys, Always say you'll try;

div.head: 'OMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: 'OMEN'S CHAT.

Royal Ifotorists.—Motoring has certainly "caught on" in Royal circles. Our own King and Queen make constant use of their many beautiful cars though it is an open secret that Her Majesty has a rooted objection to anything approaching racing. The Prince of Wales is a keen motorist and so also is the Princess Royal, while the Queen of Norway not only drives hor own car, but understands its make and mechanism. The King of Italy and the young King of Spain, are perhaps the most enthusiastic motorists among sovereigns, and in the opinion of these two monarchs, the greater the speed the better. Many people have now given up their! carriages entirely, in favour of motors, and some great I ladies prefer their chanffeurs to appear dressed as an ordinary coachmnn, especially when a footman ascom- panies the motor. Seeing the World.—Many women, longing for a , change from the monotonous routine of life, have a desire to see the world, but not everyone would care for such an adventurous career as that of Lady I Ernestine Hunt, the daughter of Lord Ailesbury. She was a hospital nurse at Krugersdorp. at the time of the Jameson Raid, but she always had a dominating passion for horses, and for the sea, and afterwards made long voyages round Cape Horn and to Australia in sailing ships. On her return she applied for a master's certifi- cate at Liverpool, but this was refused on account of her sex, so she did the next best thing, and married an °Meer on a steamer on which she travelled. Since then Lady Ernestine has once more been a nurse, and also a trainer of steeplechasers, in Ireland. More recently she has acquired a ranch in Canada, and proposes to raise thoroughbred horses. Quite lately she brought over seventeen horses to Ireland, but she bad to attend to them herself on the ship, as they were so wild that

no one else would go near them. Welsh and Irish Cottage Industries.—The Welsh ! Industries Association will hold its annual sale on ; October 15 and 1.5 at the Mansion House in London.and the Lord Mayor, and Lady Mayoress, who are both Welsh, will open the exhibition in state. Many well- known ladies have consented to preside over the various stalls, and will appear in Welsh costumes. Amongst them will be found the Duchess of Beaufort,the Duchess of Westminster, Lady Plymouth, Lady Dundonald, and it is expected that the sale of pottery, homespens, embroideries, Welsh lace, and other products of the cottage. will heat all previous records of the Associa- tion. The Irish Industries Sale will be held a fortnight later at the Philharmonic Hall in Liverpool, and is to be opened by the Duchess of Connanght accompanied by Princess Patricia. Her Royal Highness will be the , guest of Lord and Lady Derby, at Knowsley, and the house party will inclnde several distinguished Irish ladies, who will preside over the varions stalls. The Duchess of Connaught assisted by Lady Castlereagh, will sell at Lady Londonderry's stall. and Lady Aberdeen, Lady Cadogan and Lady Waterford, will all attend on the three days of the sale. Lady ondon- decry is a very earnest worker for the cause, but she has been placed in deep mourning by the recent death of the Dowager Marchioness, and it is doubtful if she will now be one of the house party at Knowsley. When the Association last held its sale at Liverpool, in leea, it realised gs,sgi a sum never exceeded at the annual sales, and altogether nearly £200.000 has been paid for Irish needlework through the medium of the Association Setting the Fashions.—Of resent years, both London and Vienna have dispnted with Paris its proud title of being the sacred city of fashion in the world. If we were required to answer the question—where do the fashions come from ?—we should probably still say Paris. but most assaredly they do not come from America, although every now and then Boston and New York try bard to set the fashions for Europe. American innovations, at a rule, are of the exaggerated type. They may have a following of a sort among certain classes, but are seldom if ever taken up by the best dressed women of London or Paris. Their colleagues on this side are therefore not much disturbed by the announce- ment that a Dressmaker's College is to be established ' in New York. This we are told, is to eventually develop into a" University of Modes," whose ambition it will be to lay both Europe and America under an interdict. and itself decide the fashionable modes for the world each season. Autumn Sales.—One by one, the leading London drapery establishments are adopting the system of holding antutnn sales, which, until recent years, flourished only amongst suburban and provincial hiiiises. To those who are expert in the art of shopping, it is a useful innovation.as the autumn overhaul of one's ward- robe generally reveals a sad deficiency in our stock of winter garments. One magas of the art of shopping, and it is a real accomplishment, as we all know among our circle of friends and acquaintances, how one will lay out her money to much greater advantage than another. But at no time is the exercise of firmness and inclement more necessary than when buying at the sales. Upon this depends whether money is saved or wasted, but to women of shopping capabilities the sales are a boon, and with foresight and the necessary ready money it is now possible to provide on these occasions, for almost one's entire requirements for the year. At the Milliners.—A curious feature in the millinery world is the new foliage, which in the majority of cases is of the same hue as the flowers with which it is mixed. For example, the fashionable red anti purple dahlias are surrounded with red and purple foliage, and curious though the innovation appears, when described, the effect on the new autumn headgear is exceedingly good. In the matter of colouring, all shades—save the natural ones—are being employed, and the dead-leaf hues, so modish in the spring, have almost disappeared. Hair dyes and Transformations.—Hairdressers tell us that transformations, and semi-transformations, are more in demand than ever before, and there is no denying the 'fact that these particulars "aids " have been brought to the utmost protection. There was a time when women were as much -ashamed of wearing "acquired " hair as our grandmothers were of wearing artificial teeth, but that period has passed, and provided a woman is not so foolish as to choose ton youthful a tint, nothing can be said against the mode. Another item of news forthcoming from the fashionable hair- dresser, is the growing tendency to leave hair dyes alone. This is a move in the right direction. Often the hair tarns grey, when its possessor is quite young, and
CHAPTER XXII.
LORD DE MORLEY'S house in Holland Park was one of the show houses of London.

It was a veritable palace built in the most modern style, with every improvement that the art of man could devise to 'make life pleasant and existence comfortable. The great hall might from its size have been that of a fashionable hotel. There were treasures that few houses in London could boast of. The bronze fountain in the centre was a masterpiece by Claus, of Innsbruck,* and the Light from the stained windows fell upon armour that had been worn by the knights of the conqueror, battle axes that had flashed at Cressy, carpets from Ispahan woven three hundred years ago and seeming still fresh from the loom. •

The de Moneys had been an old family when John in the meadow, at Runnymede penned his unwilling signature to Magna Charter. They had prospered steadily through all the years,adding to their lands, and assisted by that law of entail which makes the English aristocracy the richest and most powerful is the world.

Lord de Morley had married young and had hoped for an heir to his vat estates, Nit Providence had only sent him a daughter. His wife had died shortly after the child was born ; he had never married again, and at the date of this story Estelle, a girl of eighteen, was keeping house for him. She was an exquisite girl with pale golden haiL, and grey eyes. Greuze alone could have doffe justice to her face, which was the despair of modern painters. She had been the beauty of the la§t season when, at a ball given by the French Ambassador, Sir William Harding, one of the handsomest men in London, and the most promising of the younger politicians, had seen her and loved her at sight. A few mornings after the day on which Arthur Esmond had been released on bail Estelle de Morley was seated writing letters in the library which adjoined the great hall when her father entered. He wore a gloomy look. For the last few days he had been visibly depressed. The loss of the all important document which might be used at any moment by its finder weighed upon his spirits. It was like a bombshell that might explode at any moment and wreck Sir William Harding; himself and the party to whoni he belonged. Estelle looked up from her writing, saw her father, and putting down her pen, rose up and kissed him affectionately. She was full of plans about her forthcoming marriage which was to take place in the autumn, but busy as she was with Paquin and Redfern and the jewellers and the lulndred and one people who make the preparations for a fashionable marriage a real business, her loving eyes could not but see that some trouble weighed upon her father. "Has Harding been this morning ? " asked Lord de Morley, as he took his seat in an arm- chair and drew his cigarette case from his pocket. "Yes, he came in for a moment," said Estelle, striking a match and holding it to her father's cigarette. "He wants me to go this afternoon with him for a ride in the park. father." " Yes." "You look depressed and worried; is any- thing wrong ? " " Oh nothing in particular," he answered, watching the blue spiral curls of smoke from his cigarette. " The Government were nearly defeated last night, but you don't care about politics.? "You are not worrying about the loss of those jewels ? " " I," said he with a start ; " oh, no. I'm not worrying about the jewels; all the same it was a most provoking loss." " I'm almost glad they were lost," said Estelle, perching herself like a bird on the arm pf his chair and resting her hand lovingly upon iis shoulder. "Do you know I have been feading only this morning the history of the val." " Which opal ? " "The fire opal with the horrid inscription Dn., the back. You remember you showed it to Me before you sent it to the bank with the other jewels." 4 " Ah, yes," said her father; "so you've been reading the history of it. I remember now there as a pedigree of some sort attached to it."
"Uncle !James left you the opal, did he not ? "

. yes." "And Uncle James was drowned'at sea?" "He was," said de Morley. " Podr old James. I remember the morning he started from Southampton in his yacht as well as if it were only yesterday. I little thought I would never see him again." "Well," said Estelle, "Uncle James bought the opal at the sale of the Marquis de Sobraon's jewels." " Sobraon, the man who was stabbed in the Place VenclOrne ? "

"Yes, and the Marquis de Sobraon . had bought it from the executors of Sir Douglas Graham, of Clanboyne." " Which Graham was that, not-" "The one who killed his own brother in a duel and committed suicide."
" Good gracious, Estelle, what are all these frightful things you are telling me; you aree perfect little ghoul! "
" I am only telling you the history of the fire opal. Sir Douglas Graham had obtained it in Paris from a man. Guess how the man had obtained it."
" I can't—murdered someone for it I sup- pose." " No, he got it in exchange for a glass of water."
" A glass of water I "

" Yes, he was an innkeeper in the time of the Revolution. He was standing at his door one day when a tumbril passed by filled with wretched people going to be executed. Amidst them was the beautiful• Princess de Porcian. He gave her a glass of water at the risk of his life and she gave him the brooch; it was the fire opal. " There is a great deal more history attached to the stone, but it is a terrible history. Everyone who has died when in possession of it has come to some disastrous end. The in- scription on the back runs:

"Who holds me tempts Fate Who in darkness cloth wait; To my keepers I gave The sword and the grave; The same I give thee If my keeper thou be." s " Where did the thing come from origin- ally ? " asked Lord de Morley. Le Gros, the great French traveller, brought it to Europe from India." " Well," said Lord de Morley bitterly, " I only hope that if what you say is true, the 'present holder of it will come to some speedy and disastrous end."

" Oh, father ! " said Estelle, " don't wish that." "Not wish it, why look at the mischief the scamp has worked; that young bank clerk is ruined for life if the affair is not cleared up. They suspect him, but 'he's innocent of that I'm positive."
4 And thel poor 'girl who' ran away." said istelle. "Miss—what was her name—oh, Graham?"
"She's innocent, too," said de Morley.
" She 'wrote him Ithat letteri which memed I suspicions enough, but his explanation is "Rite plausible. She referred to an appoint- ment he had made with her in her aunt's garden." _ _ _ .
But why did She run away ? " /asked Estelle. .

" She:was ashamed, I suppose, and her aunt was a hard old woman who always treated her badly." - "Poor things," said !Estelle. She was think- ing of the two lovers, separated so sadly an:d happy in her own love;, their fate appealed to her with double force.
"Do you Iknow where this Mr. Esmond lives ? " she asked her father. '
"Yes, he lives at No. Montague Place. Why do you ask? "
"I would like to go and see him and tell him to cheer up," said the girl. " I hate to think of people unhappy when I am so happy. May I go, father ? " "Don't be a goose," said de Morley, kissing
her. " I won't," said Estelle; "but I will go and see him all the same."
She turned round. A servant had tapped at the door and was advancing with a card on a silver salver.
"A person wishes to see you, my lord," he said.
Lord de Morley took the card on which was inscribed the name, " John Forbes." Them was no address.
'Show him into my stUdy," said his lord- ship, " and I will see him,"

div.head: CHAPTER XXIII.
div.p: CHAPTER XXIII.

THE GRAFTER who had been debating the matter in his evil mind had that very morn- ing determined upon a daring stroke. When he left his room in Old Compton Street he presented a very different figure from the one he. cut on the day of Arthur's misfortune. The amiable old clergyman was now all ,Ll,;rt clean-shaven man of forty or so who had the appearance of a prosperous actor and all the air of a man about town.

He first went to. the Strand where, early as the hour was, he entered several bars, not to drink, however, for he rarely drank anything more intoxicating than lemonade, but to transact business with acquaintances. There is no place on earth perhaps where " shady " people congregate more than the Strand sand its vicinity. Betting men, racing touts, ,gamblers, all the people who live by their wits here abound and find a fruitful field for their labours.
The Grafter) having entered several bars, transacted lus business, and met two or three acquaintances—he had no friends—entered a cab and told the driver to take him to Holland Park.
He dismissed the cab' several streets away from Loryl de Nlorley's bodse and arrived at that nobleman's residence on foot.

"His lordship is at home," said the flunky who [admitted him," but I doubt if his lord- ship receives at this hour." " Just take him my card," said the Grafter, handing a pasteboard inscribed, " Joha Forbes. And please let him have it at once; my business is of importance and my time is valuable."

The inimitable " cheek " of the man was well exhibited in his calm assurance. As he waited in the hall he examined the art treasures with an appreciative eye; he tapped the border of the bronze fountain with the tip of his walking-stick and appraised the value of the wooded of Turkish rugs, calculating in his mind what they would bring if they were put up for auction. Presently the servant returned. . _
" Will You walk • this way, please ? " he said, leading the way to a door opening on the hall.
The Grafter followed and found himself i n a study lined with books and lit by a large stained glass window of exquisite design and colour.

He had, the soul of an artist and though it was allied to the mind of a villain- and the fingers of a thief, he could not but appreciate the beauty of the things around him. The books especially attracted him. Here were Elzivirs and folios of priceless value. He tried the( door of one of the book-cases, but it was fortunately locked; then he turned to the etchings (that hung upon the walls between the book-cases and examined them carefully. They were all Rembrandts. Had lyou covered eachone of them with sovereigns twice over it would not have amounted to its worth.

As; he was thus engaged the door opened and Lord de Morley entered. I. believe you desired an interview with me," said Lord de Morley, advancing with the card he had received between linger and thumb.
" I have the honour, I believe, of speaking to Lord de Morley," said the Gratter. De Morley bowed. " 1 have conic," continued his visitor, " to ask youl lutdship if I can be of any service to you.,.

- "in what way ?" •' With regard to the jewels you have lost," replied the Grafter, whose keen eyes were fixed Upon" the man belole him reading ;almost tus every thought. " The jewels I have lost I Ah, thank you, the atfau Is already in the hands of the de- tective police. 'Was it fur this that. you re- quired 40 mterview with toe? " "Yes."

" Well, I regret that. you an be of no ser- vice to me. You are a private detective 1 presume ? " " What I stn,' said Biel Grafter, "is of no affair Ito anyone but myseif. But I'll tell you ,what you are. Lord de Morley.- " What I au, " " Yes, you are a 10011"

De Morley who had made three steps to the door to .open it wilt eled round and stared at the man who had dared to, use such language to him in his own house, lie was utterly paralysed for the moment. " 1 do not in the least mean to insult you," said the Grafter quite coolly. " I mean that you are a fool in this particular instance." " Do you know whom you are addressing, sir ? " said de Morley. "Do you mean to apologise to toe this instant or will you wait till I 'call my servants to fling you into the street '? " " Call them," said the Grafter.

" 'Lshall not only call them; but T will send for a policeman." said de Morley. opening the door. " Shall I tell him about the treaty I " asked the Grafter, taking a seat in an tarm- chair and producing his cigarette case. De Morley closed the door and turned, suddenly stricken pale as, death. " The treaty, what treaty ? " • "Ii you will give me time to explain my- self," said the Grafter, "1 will tell you all about it. It is a matter of high policy and affects your interests, and it is vital to the interests of Sir William Harding, who is, *I believe, about to become your son-in-law."
De Morley sat down; the perspiration was standing on his forehead in beads.• Go on," he said, "go on."

"I must tell you the affair in my own way." said this terrible visitor. ," To:begin with, you must know that the card 4...4e1it in to you just now bears a name which is dot mine, but all the same in this shady business let me ask you to believe that you are dealing with a gentle- man. I am a University man, or was; my father was a clergyman, but he was poor. as

many clergymen are. Excuse me for bother- ing you with details of my past history, but I have a habit of telling stories in my own way or not telling them at all. May I smoke— thanks. Well, my father was poor, but I was poorer; however, I managed to cut a pretty good figure at the college I belonged W. f. I was an expert billiard player and cards were ray forte. I also studied men. Between billiards, cards, and men I managed to live. But though I lived a gay life, I did not lead a senseless one. I read much; mathematics and the allied sciences were my favourite pur- suit, ancl amidst other things I went deeply into the science of cryptography. "I can say with the late lamented Edgar Allan Poe that there is not a cryptogram in- vented by man that I cannot read." "Go on," said de Morley, wiping his fore- head.

"Since leaving the University," went on the Grafter, "I have lived by virtue of my wits. I am often] consulted about cyphers. and the other day I was consulted about a writing of this sort that gave me much trouble.
" It_ was the draft °I a secret treaty—a most alarming document from a political point of view." .

" How ? " said de Morley. The Grafter s smiled. ' Well it is simply the record of a conspiracy between two nations to set upon a . third under given circumstances. That is nothing, of course, in politics; these sort of treaties are arranged every day, but there are circumstances that make this par- • ticular treaty wrong 'in a moral way. In fact," said the Grafter pleasantly, "if the present possessor of that document .were to send it to some paper, ' The Times,' let us say, the present Government would be out of office in twenty-four hours and the men re- sponsible for the treaty wcrttlet be impeached." " No newspaper would print such a thing." " Indeed they would. Its bona-fides are all right ; it is written on Foreign Office paper', and there us a pencilled note in your hand- writing, my lord, on the margin." De Morley leaned back in his chair; he was stricken .hard, but he put a brave face on the matter.
"Failing that Course," chntinued tne other, "it could be sold." " Sold I "
"To a certain foreign government. Your lordship must know that political secrets, real ones, are as valuable rand as saleable as diamonds."
"I suppose so. Do you know in whose possession this document is now ? " "I may be able to find out." " How was it obtained ? " "It was found, I believe, in a bag with some jewels." _ . . . .
"Surely the finder might keep the. jewels and, return the document."
" Good :gracious 1" ,said the Grafter, "what a strange proposal 1"
"Why! the document is of more value than the jewels." " The jewels,l' • said de Morley, " were worth, I believe, forty thousand pounds."

"That was their stated value. To a thief they 'would not be worth more. than five. You have never sold stolen jewellery, my lord, or you would know how the fence grinds the poor thief down. It is a regular system of :sweating, and there ought to be a Royal Commission of enquiry into it." Lord Ide Morley did not notice' this pleasantry; the was seated: with his head bent tracing the pattern of the carpet with his eyes. He was debating as to how he should act. . .

The Grafter, on his side, was watching his . adversary narrowly. He knew. he had the man before him in a net, so to speak, and he determined to make the most of the situation. , Suddenly Lord de Morley raised his head. " This document is for sale ? " he said. " I believe so." "I will buy it back." "It would be prudent to do so." " Name the price." "Ten thousand pounds." "Ten thousand pounds ? " "Not a farthing less, it is a to* price con- sidering that your lordship's income is a thousand a day."
" I will pay it on receipt of the document. When can I have it 2 " " Immediately." . " How ? " • " It is in my pocket." " Show me it, and, if it's what I seek I will give you a cheque." " . . . '
- " f trust your lordship's honour implicitly," said the Grafter. /

He put his hand in the breast pocket of his coat and produced a.. small 'brown paper parcel tied with string. He opened the parcel carefully. There was notEing in it but some; pieces of newspaper and two small biscuits.
Well? "I. said de Morley, looking on in astonishment.

div.head: FLORENCE NIGHTINGALE.
div.p: FLORENCE NIGHTINGALE.

'When the heroine of the Crimea was a little girl, she one day saw a shepherd's dog badly injured by some stones thrown by thoughtless boys. It was decided that the poor animal must be killed. But Florence went up to him and patted his head, and at last coaxed him into letting the Vicar of the parish examine his leg._ _

"There are no bones broken," he said, "but he is badly bruised. The leg ought to be fomented to take the inflammation and swelling down." "How do you foment ? " asked Flgrence. "With hot cloths dipped in boiling water," answered the Vicar.
" Tlon that's quite easy. I'll stay here and do it.

And so Florence Nightingale made her first compress, and spent the whole of that bright spring day in nursing her first patient—the shepherd's dog. In the evening, when the shepherd came, not expecting to find visitors in the humble cottage, and dangling a bit of cord in his hand, Florence wen* up to him. "You can throw that away, Roger," she said; "your dog won't die; look at him!" And Cap rose and crawled towards his master, whining with pleasure.
"Deary me! Cleary me! What have you done with him?" And when Florence told him what she had done—
"Thank you kindly, I do indeed," he said. "I'll see to him, missy, now as I know what's to be done."; and he stood his crook in the corner and hung his cap on the peg.

GLASS THAT KEEPS OUT HEAT RAYS.

Ordinary window glass passes nearly all of the heat coming from the sun, but the new glass of Richard Szigmondy, an Austrian, is claimed to prevent the passage of ,i-te•teriths of the heat of the sun's rays. This would change a hot- house into a cold-houte. The advantages seem to be numerous, but not least should be the de- lightful coolness of summer cottages having win- dows of the new material.

div.head: PAPER GAS PIPES.
div.p: PAPER GAS PIPES.

An interesting employment of paper relates to the production of gas pipes. Manila paper cut in strips, of a width equal to the length of the pipes to be made, is put in a receiver filled with fused asphalt and rolled 'solidly and uniformly around a rod or core of iron until the desired thickness is obtained. After the pipe thus pro- duced has been submitted to strong pressure, the exterior is covered with sand and the whole cooled in water. The core is removed and the outer surface covered with a waterproof product. These pipes, it. appears, are perfectly tight and snore economical than metal pipes.

div.head: SIZE OF OCEAN WAVES.
div.p: SIZE OF OCEAN WAVES.

In an article published in the Revue Seien- tifique, M. Bertin, the well-known naval archi- tect, maintains that the heights and, lengths of ocean waves are often greatly over-estimated. The most reliable method of determining the length is, he states, to deduce it from its period, since there is a simple relation between this length and the time of complete oscillation. The longest wave of which he has cognisance is 800 metres (2,590 ft. from crest to crest, its period being 23sec. These long waves, he states, are never very high. In deep water the height of a wave, 800 metres long, will not, at most, be more than 16 metres, or one-fiftieth its length. Much greater heights than this have, he says, been recorded, particularly from small craft, but the observations were quite unreliable.

div.head: ELECTRIC WAR ON MOSQUITOES.
div.p: ELECTRIC WAR ON MOSQUITOES.

M. Maurice Chaulin, of Paris, has declared war, electrically, on mosquitoes and gnats. He proposep to replace the old methods by electro- cution, thanks to an apparatus which he has in- vented and patented. A cylindrical lantern is constructed of two rings suspended one above the other and connected by parallel and vertical chains. These are connected with the .source of electricity, in such a fashion that each of the chains is always alive. In the centre is a lamp. Electric or other light attracts mosquitoes, which begin to buzz around the lamp and come into contact with the chains. The moment an inseet touches two at once with its legs it estab- lishes a short circuit, and is immediately electro- cuted. If this apparatus be installed in a bed- room it has only to be lighted a' short time before the owner retires, to insure a quiet night's sleep.

DURATION OF FLASHES OF LIGHTNING. We possess as yet only pretty vague data as to the average duration of flashes of. lightning, says L'lllustration. Faraday thought he could fix it at a second. Duf9ur claimed that the flashes of lightning were instantaneous, and that their rapid succession gave the Illusion of one flash of a certain' duration. Herr Schmidt has just been devoting himself to a sevies of observations, employing • a disc of ten centi- meters diameter bearing upon A black ground a white cross, the arms of which were two milli- meters across, the disc being set in motion by clockwork with a speed of fifty to sixty revolu- tions a second. At certain flashes, the cross ap- peared a single time, very distinct; the dura- tion of lightning was, therefore, inferior to the time of revolution of the disc, which would re- present about the fiftiegi of a second. In more numerous caSes, the cross appeared two or three times, or even more, but with a decreas- ing luminous intensity; the lightning had, therefore,, lasted during several revolutions of the disc.

div.head: ELECTRICALLY – CONDUCTIVE GLASS.
div.p: ELECTRICALLY - CONDUCTIVE GLASS.

Experiments have from time to :time been made, both in England and abroad, to ascer- tain what ingredients are best for the purpose of producing glasses of very high electrical re- sistance, says a writer in rature. The utility of a vitreous substance which would conduct elec- tricity comparatively well does not appear, however, to have so far claimed any considera- tion. Attention should be directed to a glass which has recently been made in my labora- tory. Its chief feature is ;that it really conducts electricty. For the windows or cases of electro- scopes and all high-tension apparatus requiring a transparent cover capable of screening off ex- ternal electrical fields, this material' offers many advantages. A conducting varnish is no longer required for glass which conducts elec- tricity itself. In addition to these practical con- siderations, there arises the interesting ques- tion as to the process by which electricity passes through this substance--whether it is electrolytic. Its resistance varies very markedly with temperature changes. The basis of the glass is sodium silicate.

div.head: MENTAL CAPACITY .OF WOMEN.
div.p: THE MENTAL CAPACITY .OF WOMEN.

In the opinion of Dr. B. Hollander, the mental power of a woman is not in the least inferior to that of man. But she is dissimilar, hence differ- ences of result. As the !lector forcibly pointed out, all work, mental or otherwise, is directed by motive, and just because a woman is of distinctly emotional character, what she needs and what she constantly seeks is to gain happiness through her feelings rather than by the exertion of her intellect. This being so, it naturally follows that while she may be the intellectual equal of man, the motive to exert her thinking faculties to the same extent does not exist. On "woman's rights" Dr. Hollander hblds emphatic views. In the relation of man and woman he thinks there is no question of rights and duties, ordination or snbordmation, boundaries or restraints, but only a question how far their natures can merge into one another. All " rights " between man and wife are merely, in his opinion, defences— weapons of protection against unfortunate unions. The emancipation of woman he regards as siinply woman's despair of herself as a woman. The true antidote to the woman clues- don he believes is for parents to see that their daughters are married, instead of bringing them up for "freedom." which means flirtation, but not marriage. Moreover, Dr. Hollander believes that the up-bringing, of girls is responsible for their seeking an occupation instead of marriage. Unfortunately, in his opinion, the struggle which such.women have frequently to endure rouses the darker 'passions, produces the worry which is al- ways closely connected with work, and soon the i r,al working girl finds that Ihe s plainer than when\ she was at home. div.head: NEGRO BRAIN.
div.p: THE NEGRO BRAIN.

The negro race is now oonsidered, says a writer in the Ccrtury, to be one of the oldest races in the world, evidences of its existence in prehistoric times having been recently discovered throughout Africa, Australia and Oceana. In historic times nemroes are depicted on the monu- ments of Egypt thousands of years before the Anglo-Saxon had emerged from barbarism. They have been in contact continually with the high- est civilisations of antiquity, but have never risen to the eminence of other nations, having re- tained their primitive condition, even as is now apparent in the Southern States, where they an isolated in large masses. Another significant fact is that the negro brain is smaller than the Caucasian, the difference in sine being represented in both grey matter (nerve (ells) and white matter (nerve fibres). Brain cellt are the basis of brain power or mental ability, and their number is known to remain constant throughout life, so that there is never mental development beyond the possible expression of the brain cells inherited. Development of mental activity by experience, education, dtc., if considered to be correlated with the development of sheaths around, till nerve ,fibres, as they be- come active in the tran,mission of impulses. The efficiency of the brain depends upon the numbez and position of such nerve fibres, just as the efficiency of a telephone system depends upon the number of its various connections and mini& cations. The negro brain having fewer nerve cells and nerve fibres, _assuming that grey rnattei and white matter respectively represent these numerically the rwmihilitios of deyeloninir The rivro are therefore limited, except by crossing with other races. This has been done to sunk an extent in times past that it is difficult to do termine whether a pure negro really eixiete ii America.

LADY OWNERS OF CP.EYHOIINDS.

More greyhounds are now owned by women than has been the case since the establishment of the National Coursing Club, • but there is no record of greyhounds owned by ladies being at the end .of an important produce stake until the other day, when, on the Everleigh Downs, Lady Arthur Grosvenor's Cora Lee and Miss Ruth Fawcett's Ruby Foyle divided the Collingbourne Stakes. 'Miss. Fawcett has taken- an active inte- rest in coursing for years, and in the days of the old Cirencester Club it was her habit as a school- girl to take her 'own greyhounds to the slipper, and to "pick up her dog after a course. It was at one of the Hampshire meetings that she was given an ovation for refusing to divide a stake because of approaching darkness, and the doubt there was that a hare might not be found for the ' deciding course. One was found, and Miss Faweett's g.reyhou,ld won. Miss Fawcett is the daughter of a Cotswold clergyman, who also owns a few greyhounds.

div.head: BLACU-ANDWIIITE.
div.p: BLACU-ANDWIIITE.

Each autumn sees the 'revival of the magpie costume, for black-and-wane is. much too smart a combination to remain long out of favour. A good example was recently ,3cen and sketched for this column. The coat, fitting the figure and reaching a, little way below, the waist, was of fine black cloth, and had a small collar of black- and-white check cloth, folding over a little inner vest of the same which just met in front, fastening with invisible hooks and eyes. The

skirt was of the check cloth, closely pleated. and had the hem furnished with 11 broad band of the same black cloth as the coat. It would be a novel idea to reproduce this costume in the new shade known as Burgundy-red. This is to be a very popular shade during the winter, and as the season advances will be more acceptably warm-looking than the original magpie scheme.

div.head: LATEST BEAUTY FAD.
div.p: THE LATEST BEAUTY FAD.

Fashionable women are taking up fruit ate beauty diet with avidity. Fruit has alniost ousted the regulation bacon and eggs from the up-to-date breakfast-table, the fruit luncheon is a popular institution, and canteloupe melon is served as the hors-d'reuvre. The idea of using fruit and vegetables for external application in the form of lotioils made froni the juices is, how- ever, a new deillopment, says a writer in the Tribune. Carrots, .for instance, are reported to to work wonders on a muddy complexion. Rain- water in which grated carrots have been allowed to soak for an hour is applied direct to the skin. Cucumber juice possesses just enough of the bleaching properties to be most efficacious when applied to tan and sunburn. Take the outer peeling of the cucumber with just sufficient of the wilite to contain 'a little of the jtice, bind strips of peel, the soft side towards the skin, around a tanned throat, or over a sunburnt fore- head. Leave this bandage on as long as possible, and you will prove that cucumber is a fine whitener, containing just enough arsenic to make it valuable as a cosmetic: TrssoKE SILK BLousn.

The blouse which forms the subject of our sketch is a simply-made little affair in tussore silk, dyed a particularly penetrating shade of blue, something between a peacock and a royal, and known usually as sea-blue. It is a most effective colour, and one that tussore takes to perfection. The blouse is perfectly plain exoept for tho plastron effect down the front. Thisii

formed of a deep V-shape of the silk, tom- bined with a central band or box-pleat, the whole being embroidered in rich autumn tints of terra-cotta. TINA most invaluable trimming the ready-made • kilted silk frill, about an inth wide, is used for edging the embroidered plas- tron, and the short puff sleeves are finished to correspond. The V-shape is repeated down the back, but the central band in omitted on ac- count of the fastenings. MAISAME MELBA AS PIANIST.

BLACICBERRY TRIFLE.—Select only the ripest blackberries. Line a deep glass dish, bottom and sides, with the fruit, sprinkle liberally with sugar, and prepare the following custard: Beat the yolks of four eggs and one whole egg till light, and then mix iM soz. of castor sugar, and beat in by degrees a pint of milk, hot, but not boiling. Place in a jug, stand in a saucepan of boiling water on the fire, and stir rapidly until the custard thickens. Then remove quickly,lset aside to cool a little, and then add a dessert- .n.conful of strained lemon ivice. Before it is quite cold and set pour into the centre of the blackberries, and just before serving lay a sponge-cake in thin slices over the custard, cover with more blackberries, and pile whipped cream on the top.

TBAMWAYS COMMITTEE. RETURN FARES.

• The committee resolved "that the resolution of this committee of the 11th instant referring to id. return tickets be rescinded ; that the Council be recommended to rescind the resolution of 3rd July relating to work- men's fares, and that the following regulations with regard thereto be recommended to the Council for their approval :—(1) That id. return tickets be issued from each terminus within the borough before 8 a.m. on any day except Sunday, the return half to be available on any journey and any route between the hours of 5 and 8.30 p.m. on any day except Saturday and Sunday; (2) that on Saturdays the return half be available between the hours of noon and 2 p.m." . _ _

Alderman SMETHURST moved theconfirmation of the minutes of the committee, and observed with refer- ence to the Warrington and Northwich Light Railway, "that the committee did not intend to be let in for any cost of working that establishment." The question of the return tickets had given the committee a very great deal of anxiety and trouble and even then they would not be able then to give satisfaction to all. It was thought a certain class had been omitted who were more deserving of consideration than those who got large wages, and that class was composed of girls and men who served behind the counter at a salary of from £2.00 to 255. a week. All cheap tickets must now be bought before eight o'clock a.m.' and the buyer could return by it on that day or any clay afterwards, so long as the date was on, and the ticket was kept clean. He thought the present arrangement would be a great relief to a large number of inhabitants. Many of the shops did not close until eight o'clock and, there- fore, the time had been extended for using the tickets. Councillor WILKINSON seconded. Councillor AsHcnorr: Will the resolution include clerks?
Alderman SMETHURST.: Everyone who gets a ticket before 8 a.m.

Councillor WrLsos said the labouring man who 18s. a week h. been forgotten. A workman going from Latchford to Sankey Bridges would have to pay 2d., and he moved, therefore, that the resolution with reference to the fares be deleted. A man who wanted a half-penny ride should have it either way he wished. With halfpenny fares the ears were full whilst with the return fares the cars were empty. Councillor BARTON seconded, and said the present proposal did not suit a number of men at Sankey Bridges, who did not leave off work until nine o'clock. . . .
, The MAYOR: We might stretch it another. hal f-ho ur. We thought we had included everyone. We do not want to take anything out of the working man, but we don't want to do an injustice to others.

Councillor WrlxiNsoN said the committee had gone , a stage further than was at first proposed, and issued ' tickets at either end, so that a person living in a sub- urban district, and working in the town, could be accommodated. (Hear, hear.) A puddler who went to Monks, Hall got his penny ticket, and if he came back at night he was all right. The object of the resolution was to take in all classes of people earning from 18s. a week—girls, boys and tnen—and giving them an oppor- tunity of going ti. their work. He claimed that it met every point that could be brought forward. There WAS no limit to the keeping of the half-penny ticket. It might be kept for five years. (Laughter.) Co,mcillor PENIBERTON : What sort of a state would the ticket be in ? (Laughter.) Councillor WILKINSON: Don't be silly. We cannot expect to keep towels and soap to wash workmen's hands. (Renewed laughter.) The MAYOR : The principal reason why the resolu- tion was passed was that we wanted to get rid of the friction that occurred. In the ordinary wayt the con- ductor had to say who is a workingman, and if a man came up in collars and cuffs and claimed a halfpenny fare friction arose.

Councillor BALL said he felt disposed to support the resolution, and not the amendment. The result of the continued deliberations of the committee had been a regulation which, in his opinion, applied the most fairly all round. They would never be able to meet the wishes of every section. Councillor MAGI-Ns objected to interference from outsiders as to the work of the committee, and said he believed they had done fairly well, considering the experience of the past. For three years there had been a dead loss on the working of the trams, but they had just made a profit. It was small, certainly, but it showed an improvement, and for outsiders to air their views at the loss of the general ratepayer, was an insult to the Tramways Committee. Before they gave everything to the pudier who worked over-time at Sankey Bridges they should consider the possibilities of providing facilities fur those parts of the town which up to the present had not been considered at all. On a vote being taken the amendment was lost and the minutes approved. LAMPLIGHTERS' WAGES. REDUCTION NOT APPROVED.

At a meeting of the Gas Committee it was resolved „jhat lamplighters be paid 21s. per week of six days, and that they be paid 2s. for Sunday work. Councillor WRIGHT took exception to the minute and moved that it be not confirmed. The proposal in effect meant the reduction of the wages of the men by 2s. 2d. h. week. Even then it was not in accordance with the Standing Orders, es, making an allowance for work on Saturday afternoon, the wages were only 20s. Bd. a week. Councillor STOTT seconded. The amendment was carried by a large majority. FIRE ENGINE COMMITTEE. In moving the adoption of the minutes of the Fire Engine Committee Councillor BURTON explained that the Committee bad waited upon Messrs. J. Crostield & Sons with a view to their engines being used if necessary to assist the Warrington Engines during repairs to the steam engine "Major." Messrs. Crostield willingly promised their assistance. The Borough Surveyor had been instructed to ascertain the cost of instlnteoes couplings to replace those at present in use. It was You important that the Council should agree that night to the change of the couplings as the makers of the chemical fire engine desired to know what size of couplings were to be used. It was also ftn opportune time to make alterations to the fire engine " Major " whilst it was undergoing repairs. Councillor PEMBERTON objected to any money being spent on the couplings as there was nothing on the minutes about them. • The MAYOR: If, there is nothing on the minutes what does it matter if they are carried. Councillor PEMBERTON : There is something behind this. The Chairman of the committee wants the Council to grant the spending of the money. The MAYOR: When the estimates are obtained they will come before the Council for confirmation. Councillor PEMBERTON : That is not what the Chair- man wants. The minutes were approved. THE PRINTING OF THE MINUTES. A NEW STANDING ORDER. Councillor LORD moved: That Standing Or der No. 9 be rescinded and that the following be substituted therefor:—"That all minutes of Cmpnittees shall he printed upon the Council Agenda and the Chairman of each Committee shall determine which of such minutes shall be kept from the Press." He said the old standing order had been abused, as was evidenced by the fact that the Birtles and Elelsten property .purchase had been arranged and salaries had been raised without she whole Council being aciu tinted of the proceedings. Councillors could Inspect the written minutes of any committee, but was it fair that they should be expected to get a knowledge of Corporation business by examining eighteen minute boobs. div.head: COUNT WARD AND COPPER.
div.p: COUNT WARD AND COPPER.

Count Ward, who is so well-known in London social circles, and who was largely interested in the introduc- tion of the highly successful copper companies known as Utah Consolidated and Boston Consolidated, and who is a potent factor in the copper world, is now about introduce the Utah-Bingham Mining Company here. The £1 shares of the Utah Consolidated and Boston Consolidated stand respectively at the very high figures of £l3 10s. and £6 10s., and the Utah Bingham Company appears likely to also achieve a great suoces. The total area of the property comprises about 115 acres. The claims can be almost entirely worked by tunnels, and have already been opened up and consider- ably developed. The managing engineer reports that there are already three distinct fissure veins proved,and that there is every prospect of the property. becoming one of the best in the Bingham camp. Various assays give values as high as 30 dol. to the ton The approximate value of Bingham smelting ores gives an average of' 21 per cent. to 3 per cent, of copper, in addition to gold and silver values, and they also frequently carry a very high percentage of lead andiron making them p.actically self-fluxing and thereby largely reducing the cost of smelting. The capital of the company is 2,000,000 dol. in 40e,000 folly-paid shares of sdol. each, and, in view of the great success of the other companies in which Count Ward is interested, these appear to be an attractive pm.- chase.—Advt.

She was taken to a neighbouring hospital, where the coins were dis- covered in an operation, but the child lost its life from inflammation set up by the coins, so a doctor explained at the inquest.

div.head: JUNIOR LIBERALS
div.p: JUNIOR LIBERALS
NEIN

div.head: OPENING OF THE WINTER SESSION.
div.p: OPENING OF THE WINTER SESSION.

The winter session in connection with the Warrington Junior Liberal Association opened on Monday when promise was afford4d of increased activity on the part of this progressive body. F )rmed twelve months ago the Association was early called upon to take part in a parliamentary election and the rn,erabers undertook the work alf campaigning with an enthusiasm which com- pensated for any. laak of experience and which contri-

imted in no small degree o the triumph of Liberal forces in Warrington. With active political warfare temporarily suspended attention will now be turned to educative work such as will eminently befit the young men to take their part in future contests. Monday's meeting was held at the King's Cafe, and it was hoped that the Association would be favoured by a visit fro ii its President, Mr. A. H. Crostield, 1.P., but illness prevented his attendance, and in his absence the chair was taken by Nit% William Roberts, J.P. Letters of anology for non-attendance were received from the Revs. John Youge, -and C. Harvey Cook, Aldermen Tinnion and Pierpotnt, Councillor Barton, Mr. C. Jackson Holmes and Mr. H. Roberts. SECRETARY'S REPORT.

In presenting his annual report, Mr. H. Gct.y said the Association had its birth at an unprecedented epoch in the triumphal march of the nation's progress, and could be truthfully said to be progressing favourably. They, however, had to avoid the danger of counting their strength hy show of hands, realizing that it was in the depth of fervour and design of its members that the strength of the Association was to be found. The momentuous issues of the last election, leading on the one side to retrogressive measures, frought with great evils brought out the activity or their members. (Hear, hear.) It was with regret that he had to record the resignation of their past president, Mr. E. Osborne. The Association owed him no small debt of gratitude for his splendid initiative and zeal for the welfare of their body. The Association rejoiced in the splendid 'fact that the Government had honestly tackled the muddle left behind by the last Government and within a few short months there were not wanting distinct signs of the coming of a better day. Hapily the fabric of a false imperialism Was crumbling away before the oncoming of a saner and more humanized view of life, Our foreign affairs appeared to be in a state , of comparative tranquility whilst at home I great expectations were moving in the hearts of men towards a true social emancipation and they rejoiced in the Government's aspirations towards the distant light. He trusted that in their zeal for reform they would prevent the breeding of a bitter class resentment for its pernicious influence would certainly weaken their broad, moral and ethical grasp 1 of social problems. They trusted that their members would fling themselves into the work with a lofty and absortiing faith in the ultimate success of the true principles of Liberalism and furnish examples of political strenuousness for the translation into fact of the great virtues of equity and social justice. (Applause.) Mr. J. HAWTHORN presented the financial statement which showed that the Association closed its first year with a substantial kalance in hand. Mr. WILLIAM ROBERTS said there was no branch of the Liberal party of which he more cordially approved than the Junior Liberal Association which he believed would produce most telling results in years to come. He hoped the association had come to stay and that before very long they would find it possible to have a permanent home in the shape of a Junior Liberal Chili. (Applause). The reports were unanimously adopted. Mr. J. HAWTHORN moved; That this Association wishes to record its approval of the measures intro- duced by the Government during the past session and trusts that the Government will have a lone. term of office in order to secure for the country much needed reforms." (Applause.) They were living in times when politics were moving very quickly on the stage and they must not forget that the enemies of Free Trade had consolidated their forces. Interested manufacturers were scattering money very freely to support the tariff reform propaganda in the hope that they would refs), a golden harvest in tariffs.' One could not held but think that if the same enthusiasm and money were expended ' in adapting themselves to the timee and in applying science, the manufacturers would do more for their industries than would be possible under a system of protected tariffs. They as Liberals and Free Traders enjoyed the benefits of free trade and ought to be in a position to give solid reasons for the faith which was 1 in them and they must study the question so that they could uphold the Free Trade .standard against all corners. Something would have to be done sooner or later with the House of Lords and when the conflict came they would have to put forth all their energies to support the Government in restticting the power of the Lords. With reference to the Government's work they wanted a much better budget than the last one and hoped that Mr. Asquith would be able to no something in the way of a graduated income tax. There were other subjects which required solving and they hoped that one of the foremost of these—the land question— would he tackled by the Government. (Applause.) Mr. RATETBONE supported. Their Tory friends were organizing their forces in the hope that at the next election they would be able to oust the Liberals from their lofty position, and it therefore behoved them to closely study the questions of the day in order that they might be prepared when the time came. (Applause). Mr. W. FURNESS urged the Association to adopt a definite line of policy. Mr. E. ENGLAND said the possibilities of an Associa- tion such as that were extremely vast. He urged the study of the political history of the country, and that they should interest themselves in municipal matters so that they would be able to undertake their share of the work when the time arrived.

Mr.-I-MOit-otiaakiTlTta-t-Onei;ibject which loomed up large on the political horizon and would have to be tackled was the tendency to what was called Socialism. In England we had a population which lacked knowledge through absence of proper educational facilities and which consequently was susceptible to being led astray by certain fallacies and it must be the object of an association like the Junior Liberal Association to educate the people to a proper understanding of things. There was a great difsculty in trying to arrive at the difference between Socialism and Liberalism. If the idea of the old Socialists had been carried out people would now be living in something like gigantic workhouses and their daily lives would resemble the daily lives of soldiers and be thought they would agree that they did not want that. He asked what right a man living in present times had to imagine a state of society many years hence and to work for that alone? Liberalism must have an open mind on all questions as there were many things which were now regarded as genuine reforms which might eventually be found not to be the unmixed blessings which it was imagined they would be. (Applause.) s Councillor EvANs also supported the resolution and urged the members of the association t 3 work with the sole object of leaving the world a little better, politic- ally and in every other sense, than they found it. The resolution was carried. - I A vote of thanks to Mr. Roberts for presiding con- cluded the meeting. During the evening refreshments were served.

div.head: Motor Car and Cycle in Collision.
div.p: Motor Car and Cycle in Collision.

On' Saturday afternoon,a somewhat serious accident happened at the corner of Palmyra-square and Bold- street. Mr. and Afrs. Jones of 19, Kendrick-street,were cycling down Bold-street,and at the same time a motor car, owned and driven by Mr. Fred Firth, 37, Peru- broke-place, Bootle, came along the square. On approaching Bold-street Mr. Firth sounded his horn. Mr. Jones crossed over the tram lines and Mrs. Jones was following, when she lost control of her machine. To avoid running her down, Mr. Firth turned his motor car suddenly on to the footpath but at the same time caught Mrs. Jones's machine. The cyclist was thrown off, but fortunately escaped injury. The motor car collided with the residence of Dr. Joseph, making a small hole in the wall, and smashing one of the valuable motor lamps.
The United Irish League of America raised £14,00) in 20 minutes for Home Rule at its convention, and £20,000 is promised.

div.head: HARVEST FESTIVALS.
div.p: HARVEST FESTIVALS.
CAIRO-STREET C.IAPEL, WARRINGTON.

The harvest thanksgiving services in connection with the above chapel were held on Sunday. The building had been most effectively decorated for the occasion, the best and the most elaborate work being that at the pulpit and over the communion table. Special music was rendered. the choir acquitting themselves admirably in the anthems. Mr. James Muir presided at the organ. The pulpit was occupied morning and evening by the Rev. Charles Harvey-Cook, who in the evening preached from the wosds : "Asif a man should cast seed into the ground, and should slee,), and rise night and day, and the seed should spring up affd grow up, he knoweth not how," St. Mark iv. 26 and 27. The harvest, he said, whs mystery, the mystery of the theologian, but a mystery that kindled intelligence and reverence. With all the researches of the philosophers, no one had been able to tell them the whole story of a grain of wheat. Nature allowed them to see so much and no more. These harvest times showed them the garments of God, and if they loved Him they would love and study His works. He could not imagine people saying they loved God, and yet did not love the robe He dressed films; in, and though some things they might not know, y what was to be known they ought to seek to kno . Their love of God lutist be more than the love of their heart ; it most be the love of their mind. The collec- tions were in aid of the District Nursing Association. ST. MARY'S CHURCH, GREAT SANKEY.

The thanksgiving services were held in this church .on Sunday. The morning service was conducted by the Vicar and the Rev. fl. P. Hiscoke, vicar of SL Ambrose Church, Simm's Cross, occupied the pulpit, and preached. In the afternoon s children's flower service took place, when the Rev.J.R.Joues gave an address. In the evening the Rev. F. S. Crane, vicar of Sutton, preached, the Church being filled in every part. During the day special anthems and hymns were sung by the choir. The decora- tions were on an elaborate scale, fruit, flowers, and cereals having been used with much effect by the Nlisses Tinsley, Mrs. Gilbert, Miss Daunt, Miss Ellison, the Misses Jeans xi iss Gilbert, Miss Jones,-- Miss Hodgkinson, Miss Warborton, and Miss A. Warburton. The offertories frekr the day amounted to £26 68. 6d., and will be devoted to church expenses. PENKETEI WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

Harvest thanksgiving services were held in the above place of worship on Sunday. The morning service was conducted by the Rev. John Gunnell, who also preached Hymns were sung, and the solos in the anthem were taken by Miss E. Plimpton and Miss Johnson. Tbe evening service was conducted by the Rev. E. J. flawne' who preached to a crowded congregation. Harvest hymns were chosen, and the solos of the anthem were sung by Mr. Frank Irelang and Miss Connie Atherton. Mr. George NV. Weaver presided at the organ. The interior of the sacred edifice presented a most pleasing appearance being lavishly decorated with fruits, The collections were in advance of last year, and were equally divided between local and oonnexional funds.

THE exports of iron and OUR WONDERFUL steel from the United IRON AND STEEL Kingdom during the EXPORTS present year form the most complete reply to the report of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S Tariff amumis sion that could possibly be imagined. While we were told that Germany and the United States had ousted us from the world's iron mark3ts, the actual fact is that the quantity of British iron and steel sent abroad this year largely exceeds that of any other country. In the eight months, January —August, no less than £53,589,000 worth, includ- ing ships, cutlery, and machinery,but not including cycles . and motor cars, was shipped to foreign ' countries, which easily establishes a record in the annals of the British iron industry. If this aston- ishing rate of increase is kept up for the remainder of the year the mere increase in our iron and steel exports will amount to £16,157,000 and the total volume to E 30,300,000. The "Iron and Coal Trades Review,"a journal which has not been over friendly to Free Trade, not only admits that these figures show "a greater advance than has ever been made within an equally short time in the history of British trade," but it goes on to say that "Our recent progress must have confounded those not inconsiderable croakers who have argued that the old country was about played out." This wonderful expansion of British iron and steel exports has, not unnaturally, not been alto- gether welcome to some Tariff Reformers connected with the iron trade. Thus, at the:annual meeting of Messrs. GUEST, KEEN and NETTLEFOLD, the Chairman, Mr. Aaraua KEEN, who was a member of the Tariff Commission, declared that the prosperity of the iron trade was due to the fact that "foreign competitors were very busy, and in consequence they, at present, were able to com- pete more successfully and on better terms than than they had been able to do for some time past.' The same view was expressed in almost identical language at the annual meeting of Messrs. PEARSON AND KNOWLES, Limited, last Thursday. It is, Of course, true of all general revivals in the world's trade, But it is quite inaccurate to assert, as is sometimes done, that Germany and America in consequence of the great activity at home are not competing with us in the world's markets. As showing that the export activity of the United States has undergone no diminution, the official figures—showing that during the year ending June 30, 1906, the American iron and steel exports increased from £28,066,000 to £33,539,000 —prove that that country has by no means neglected its foreign markets. Although, too, the value of German exports has, since March 1 last, not been published, the quantities of iron and steel exported from January to June show a con- siderable increase on last year's figures, viz. 1,776,000 tons, as against 1,489,000 tons.

There can, therefore, be no kind of doubt that in taking the leading position as the greatest exporters of iron and steel the British iron trade has not been particularly favoured by the slackness of competition on the part of its rivals in other countries. This amazing proof of its ability under a Free Trade system to out distance all its competitors in capturing the world's markets lends point to the utterance of Mr. BOMAR LAW at the West of Scotland Iron and Steel Institute at the end 0f,1901, when he declared that" we ought to realise that the world's trade was always increas- ing, and that we would always get our fair share of it." In his letter to the iron workers of East Denbigh, Sir Huon BELL emphasised the value of our Free Trade policy to our foreign trade in iron and steel. He appealed to them "to consider how great is the importance of Fiscal freedom to those of us engaged in that branch of industry. It stands among the greatest exporting trades in the country. To interfere with our Fiscal policy means to hamper our foreign trade, and the first industries to suffer would be those whose prosperity depends on export. To Great Britain, whose people rely upon their food from overseas, the decline of our exports means, in the long run, a smaller quantity of food at dearer prices. The mass of the people would therefore suffer. On the iron workers the change would press in two ways—first, they would have less work and less wage, and next, dearer food with less money to buy it." The response of the East Denbigh iron workers was to give the Free Trade candidate the greatest majority ever recorded in the constituency.

We are glad that the Mayor THE MAYOR'S is to receive an indemnity INDEMNITY. from the Corporation in respect of the action pend- ing between Col. Edelsten and the C,rporation in which he is a joint defendant. As Mayor of the borough, phen acting in perfect good faith on behalf of the ratepayers he should not be held personally liable for any legal difficulties which may subsequently aria). It is the duty of the Corporation to fight his battle and pay the bill. We doubt whether any member of the Council would dissent from this view of their collective responsibility, though there was considerable opposition on Tuesday to the resolution which stated the terms of the Mayor's indemnity. With that opposition and the reason for it, we have ni'uch sympathy. The resolution is so sweeping in its terms, it indemnities the Mayor "against all damages, costs and expenses, and any order which may be made against him," that it may quite conceivably adversely effect the Corpor ation's position when they come to defend the action. What course of reasoning the Judge might take it is not far us to presume, but with matters as they stand at present we think the Council was ill-advised to vote an indemnity of such a character. The Mayor might have been assured, in all fair- ness, that he should not,be put to any pecuniary loss by sharing in the defence of the action with- out passing a comprehensive resolution which bears so closely upon the conduct of the defence. A guarantee to his Worship in a safer form would ' have answered the purpose equally well without the possibility of prejudicing public interests.
