A. Bell M.P., toe the line by signing the L.R.C. constitution. Mr. Bell did as his friends expected he refused point blank and hit out in forcible Style against the attack which had been made ntlPen his liberty of action. All that the 'ociety •cou:d do was to decide that any fatnre candidates of theirs should put on the L.R.C. cloak and kow-tow to the Kier-Hardie group. What Mr. Ball will do is, of COurse, a matter for conjecture but it is hardly likely that the electors of Derby will allow him to °e driven out of Parliament. The Miners' Federa- ,tlen have also been face to face with the same 91!Eculty within their ranks, and the question of Joining the L.R.C. was voted upon on Thursday, the vote showing a majority against such amalga- taation of nearly 10,000 votes, though only a little More than half the total number of members voted. Lancashire, Yorkshire, Cheshire and South Wales ..re strongly in favour of joining hands with the L.R.C. and there is no doubt that the socio- political policy of the L.R.C. has made considerable headway in this part of the country during the past few years. Probably 1 a further effort will be made to secure the verdict "i4f the Miners' Federation, for the L R.C. policy is 1 decidedly one of hustle. Nevertheless there is a 1 atrong feeling of opposition to their policy through- ()tit the Trade Unions all over the country. The I ..enditions of the L.R.C. are severe, cutting (4abour men off from all indentity with or pro- tnetion of the interests of the party which has for •Itia,_ Many generations been their only champion in ka ..., House of Commons, and this fact naturally Ivelghs with a body of men like the miners, who , ve not only been historically Liberal but were a pioneers of Liberal-Labour representation. The aY matters are at present drifting intLe Labour orld seems to point to a serious conflict are long. 0-. his internecine warfare is detrimental to the Nerests of the workers, and the sooner a fight `Otoes and settles something one way dr the otner lad the better it will be for the cause of Labour.

There is, we are pleased to THE JUNIOR see, ev3ry prospect of LIBERALS, another successful session for the Junior Liberal :Association. While rejoicing in the fact that Warrington has been won for the progressive ca2lBB—and that in so signal a way—the members of this promising organization do not intend to rest on their oars. -Educational work is to be pursued with vigour during the coming winter and does syllabus—a somewhat ambitious one which credit to the Association—should provide Plenty of food for thoughtful discussion. The session opened very encouragingly on Monday evening, the attendance being large and the enthusiasm correspondingly great. There was °lfily one disappointment and that was the absence through indisposition of the esteemed President of the Association, Mr. A. H. rosfield, M.P. We cordially join with the health in wishing him a speedy return to and activity. The meeting also extended lite, sympathy to Mr. Robert Pierpoint in his long ness and sudden bereavement by the death of brother-in-law, the late Dr. Brabazon. div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

Keep your return tram-tickets clean ! They are good for five years or more if still decipherable,according to the deputy-chairman of the Tramways Committee Envolopes will not be provided, however. • The inhabitant's of Manchester-road district evidently require closbr police supervision, for an out-station is to be established there. We hope they will take , warning an avoid incarceration in the new premises. 1 • ?r., A young lady in a railway carriage the other day asked the permission of Mr. J. White, M.P., to smoke a cigarette. Onto! mere politeness he could not say her nay, but the request, he says, was certain evidence of the changes which are-coming over society. Warrington is parting with an old servant. The manual fire engine which has played a useful part in " fighting the flames " on innumerable occasions is to be " scrapped." This is one of the results of pro- gress and enterprise, as the increasing application of steam, for fire engine purposes has rendered the manual machine no longer necessary.

Our readers will regret to learn that since the House rose at the beginning of August, Mr. A. H. Crosfield, has had so much business to attend to, that it has occupied him continuously during the recess. He has, therefore, been ordered to take a complete rest until Parliament meets on the 23rd of this month, and this has prevented him keeping certain engagements which he is extremely sorry to miss. We are sure we express the general feeling when we say we hope he will soon be in the best of health and strength. o , The Rev. John Francis Matthews announces a series of addresses to men only on " Religion and Life "for Thursday evenings. There is a good deal in religion and life, and their association with one another, that the average man knows little about, and Mr. Matthews' 1 efforts to instruct him will, we hope, be rewarded with success. The titles of some of the subjects announced for consideration prove that above all things Mr. Matthews means to be understandable and practical. Young men in particular should make a point of hearing Mr. Matthews' addresses. One who was there"—at the Junior Liberals' opening meeting held at the King's Cafii last Monday, informs us that he was particularly struck with the bright look upon the faces of the members. Some of them too, showed' from the remarks which fell from their lips that they belonged to the thoughtful reading section of the community, and there can be very little doubt that if they remain together,if it is only for a few years, they will not only be a powerful factor in the Liberal Party, lsut from amongst their ranks will come men who will eventually be a moral force in the town.

CRISP AND CREAMY
The Examiner, Saturday, October 6, 1906.

Fire in Bridge Street. Considerable excitement was occasioned in Bridge street last evening, by an outbreak of fire at the work- shop of Mr. Jordan. A large crowd witnessed the operations of the File Brigade, who extinguished the flames after half an hour's work.

Brass Band Massed Performance. Sunday next, being the last performance of brass bands for the season, the followink bands will give a united performance on the Recreation Ground under the conductorship of Mr. Thomas Armstrong at 3.30 p.m : —Volunteer, Pioneer, League of the Cross, Borough, Walker's, and Leigh-street Subscription.
STILL LEADING, the "HERALD" KITCHEN RANGES arid "PEVERIL " FIRE GRATES SOle Aaent.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 t0:55, Bridge-st., Warrington.—Advt. Assessment Committee.

A a meeting of the Assessment Committee held yesterday under the presidency of Mr. A. J. Jolley, applications for the office of valuer, were considered, and out of twenty-five candidates the following three were selected to appear before the committee :—Mr. Richard R. Meacock, of Culcheth ; Mr. Joseph Brewerton, of Manchester; Mr. James Clegg, of Oldham.
BABY CARRIAGES. Latest patterns.—JS. GARLAND, 51, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Fatal Fall off a Roof.

On Tuesday morning James Wright, aged 42 years, of 20, Erwood-street, was working on the roof of Messrs. Smith's Wire Works, Hallam, when he fell to the ground, a distance of over fifty feet. He was con- veyed to the Infirmary, where it was found that he was suffering from a fractured skull, and he died in that institution on Wednesday morning.--At the inquest which was held on Thursday a verdict of "Accidental death " was returned.

PUBLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR. BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Shorthand Writers' Association. The weekly meeting of the above was held at the Winmarleigh Cafe on Wednesday evening, there being a large attendance of ladies and gentlemen, The usual speed practice was conducted at varying rates. During the latter part of the evening the President, Mr. G. J. Brown,occupied the chair. A paper entitled "Athletics and Study ' was given by Mr. C. H. Long- sham, which proved to be very interesting to mem- bers. The usual discussion followed.
PUBLIC BENEFIT, UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASAIRE.—Advt.

Licensing Changes. On Monday, at the Borough Police Court, Mr. Browne applied for temporary authority for Mr. William Dunworth, of the Rope and Anchor Inn, Buttermarket-street, to sell at the Rose and Crown Inn, Bridge-street, in lieu. of Mrs. Lang, and also for temporary authority for Sergeant William O'Keefe to sell at the Rope and Anchor Inn, until the Inland Revenue Commissioners had made their award.—The applications were granted.
LAWN TENNIS, CROQUET, and other outdoor sports.—J. S. GARLAND, 51,Bridge-st.—Advt.

Lyric Quartette Party. The Lyric Quartette Party competed at New Brighton eisteddfod on Saturday and had the honour of appearing in the final after defeating several very well-known quartettes, including the winners of the Lytham and Cardiff 'festivals. In the final however, they were defeated by the narrowest of margins, although the adjudicators spoke most highly of their rendering of the test piece, "Who is Sylvia? " (Pinsuti). The voices, they said, blended splendidly, but unfortunately the tenor was untrue on one note. The prize went to the Eifian Quartette (Birkenhead) who were third at the National Eisteddfod this year. PREMIER CYCLES, 7,8, 10, 12 and 14 guineas Cash or 18 monthly payments. Sole agent, J. S. GARLAND, 51, 53 and 55, Bridge-st.—Advt. Young Free Churchmen's League.

The—winter session in connection—with the Warring- ton young FreeChurchmen's Auxiliary opened last even- ing when the Rev.J.F.Matthews delivered an address on "The young Free Churchman and his books," at a well-attended meeting held at Bold-street Church. It was pre-eminently necessary,said Mr. Matthews, that the young Free Churchman if he wished to be in the van guard of modern progress and modern social and religious movement must be a man of books as well as of affairs and needed ta devote his attention to the intellectual life of his time as revealed in its best literature. One department of literature with which he ought to he very familiar was history and especially of that period which saw the rise and growth of the religious and civil liberties of the people. Mr. liatthews urged a general reading in addition to special subjects in order that the young men would find themselves before long well equipped to act as teachers and leaders of the minds of the next generation,

div.head: NOVEMBER ELECTIONS.
div.p: THE NOVEMBER ELECTIONS.
Probable Candidates.

There is every indication of some interesting contests taking place at the municipal elections on November Ist. Already the political parties are displaying activity and the names of probable candidates are freely men- tioned. It is possible that a " four-cornered ' fight will take place in Latchford Ward, and the elections for several other seats will, it is expected, be most interesting. The following is a list of the retiring representatives who in almost every case will be certain to again come before their constituents : Town Hall Ward Conn, J. Lord (N.T.) Howley Cour). J. Sankey (C.) Latchford Conn. W. J. Wilson (C.) Bevvsey Coun. T. Wright (Labour) Orford Coun. E. Cunnington (N.T.) St. Austin's Coun. T. H. Ashcroft (C.N.T.) Fairfield Coun, T. J. Hulse (C.) Whitecross Coun. T. Barton (L.) Councillor Hulse will not seek re-election for Fair- field Ward and Mr. J. J. Neil will stand in the Con- servative interest. We understand that Mr. Neil's candidature is acceptable to the Non-Trading Associa- tion. The Liberals have not yet selected a candidate. In Town Hall Ward it appears improbable that Coun- cillor Lord will be opposed. It was rumoured that Mr. Arthur Browne intended to contest the seat but we are informed that this is not so.

At a meeting of the Liberal Committee of Bewsey Ward on Saturday evening, Mr. J. Morton, secretary of the Progressive Labour League, was asked to become the candidate and has since intimated his willingness to fight. In Orford Ward Councillor Cunnington will again seek the suffrages of the electors as a Non-Trader. Mr. W. Pook has been adopted as the Independent Labow Party's candidate, and Mr. W. Sloane is mentioned as the probable Conservative nominee. The Liberal Com- mittee recommended Mr. Peter Peacock to the Execu- tive as a suitable candidate. but Mr. Peacock informs us that he does not intend to stand.

In St. John's Ward Councillor Maginn will again come forward as an independent, and it is rumoured that he will be opposed by Mr. T. S. Steel. Councillor Sankey will again be the Conservative, candidate in Howley. Ward, and we have not yet heard of a second candidate.

In St. Austin's Ward Councillor Ashcroft will again seek the support of the voters. The Liberal Committee have held a meeting, but the matter has been adjourned for further consideration. The position in Latchford , Ward is an interesting one. Mr. J. Hughes Hill has been selected and will stand as the Liberal candidate, and Councillor Wilson will again contest the seat in the Conservative interest. Mr. E. Walker will come gorward as an independent Non-Trader, and it is not unlikely that Mr. Edwin Plinston will stand as a Labour candidate.
Deacons' Election at Wycliffe Church.

A well attended meeting of the members of the Wycliffe Congregational Church was held on Thursday evening for the election of Church °facers. The retir- ing deacons, Messrs. P. T. Winskill, Joseph Pochnore, W. Beswick, R. Wyllie, and George Wallington, were re-elected whilst Mr. J. W. slack was elected to fill the vacancy caused by the death of the late Mr. Thomas Wallington. It was announced at the meeting that Mr. Ziba Armitage had presented individual Communion cups for the use of the members of the Church.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

FREE SPEECH AT WIDNES. Last week practically all the fines imposeet upon members of the Widnes Branch of the I.L.P. were paid. Among those who "settled up" was Mr. J. H. Standring the Labour J.P. of St. Helens. Mr. de Pres and Mr. Cowan, of Liverpool, went to gaol, but their friends paid their finet within a day or two. Mr. Seddon, the member of Parliament for the Newton Division, has not yet paid his fines, while Mr. A. E. Killip, of Birken- head, and one or two of the others summoned cannot be found by the police. LIVERPOOL NATURALISTS AT HELSBY.

The concluding field meeting of the session in con- nection with the Liverpool Naturalists' Field Club was held on Saturday, when thirty members and friends I visited Helsby and Alvanley, in ideal weather. The route chosen lay around the familiar sandstone crag overlooking Helsby, and then on to Alvanley, and back to Helsby via Horn's Mill. An interesting feature of the ramble was a visit to a cave on the hill-side, where ' luminous moss was seen in great profusion. The com- petition for the prizes offered for a basket and a spray I of wild flowers was keen. RUNCORN PARENTS' CRUELTY. _

At Runcorn, on Monday, Thomas Woodfine, labourer, and Margaret \Voodfine his wife, were charged by the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children with neglecting their four children. Mr. Linaker prosecuted for the society, and since the last hearing the baby, fourteen months old, had died. At the inquest Dr. M`Donnell said the child had lived on its own fat until no fat was left, and the child only weighed 81b. instead of 201b.—Inspector Rogers said he had paid nearly thirty visits to the prisoners' house, which was almost devoid of furniture, and frequently there was no food or fire, and the children were ill-clad. The prisoners were drunken and dissolute, and the husband badly abused the wife.—The magistrates said it was the worst case there had been in Runcorn, and sentenced each prisoner to six months' bard labour. The Clerk sub-niiTied--th-e—in.llO;i4; report of Mr. Dansey's statement of pauperism and expenditure for the half-year ending Lady Day 190 G : Pauperism : the number of paupers chargeable to the Runcorn Union as compared with the corresponding period of 1903 showed a decresse of 31. The percentage of pauperism was in Mr. Dansey's whole area 2.3, county of Chester 2.0, Runcorn Union 1.8. There were six unions in Cheshire I with a higher percentage of pauperism than the Run- corn Union and three with a lower. The cost per head of population was is. 71d., county of Chester 15.7 d., and Runcorn Union is. 31d. There were seven unions in Cheshire with a greater cost per head than Runcorn and three with a less cost. RELIEVING OFFICERS' SNLIRIES.

The Cleik read an application from Mr. W. R. de Prez, relieving officer for the Budworth district, for an increase oesalary. Mr. de Prez pointed out that in the 32 years which he had held the position he had only had one advance, and that nearly twelve years ago. He also explained that the parishes of Grappenhall, Latchford Without and Thelwall had been added to the district since then without his receiving any extra remuneration. To cover his distriet efficiently he had to keep a conveyance, which practically reduced his income by £3O a year. The application wa3 refe:red to a special committee which was appointed to consider a similar application from Mr. Pearson.
The Chairman gave notice that at the next meeting of the Council he would move that Mr. Pearson's salary be increased by 10 per annum in accordance with the decision of the special committee.
-COST OF OUT-RELIEF.
The Finance Committee reported the payment in out- relief of .£7O to Mr. Cork, £3O to Mr. Pearson and ;£29 to Mr. de Prez.
RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Dis- trict Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday when there were present : Messrs. G. Pilling (presiding), T. Baxter, S. Woodwood, T. Wright, C. E. Linaker, C. E. Linaker, jun., J. B. Chadwick, J. Hallows, C. Roylance, J. Spruce, H. Eyes, J. Whitley, J. Bolshaw, J. H. Davies, A. Broome, H. Mawdsley, H. M. DAV ies, E. Bretherton and R. Billington, G. F. Ashton (clerk) J. Swinton and W. Diggle (surveyors), J. Farrington (inspector) and Dr. Adams, (medical officer.)

div.head: DUST -NUISANCE.
div.p: THE DUST -NUISANCE.

The Clerk str.ted that he had received a copy of a memorandum forwarded by the Cheltenham Rural District Council to the President of the Local Govern- ment Board, with reference to the findings of the Motor Car Commission.

Mr. Ashton explatued that there was a suggestion that a conference of Rural District Councillors should be held at Chester on October 13th, to consider the question. Messrs. Woodward and Antwis were appointed delegates to attend the conference. Mr. Livaker said although a motorist he was in sym- pathy with the resolution. A motor properly used was a good machine. Improperly used it was a nuisance.

div.head: SMALL-PDX -HOSPITAL.
div.p: SMALL-PDX -HOSPITAL.

The Clerk reported the receipt of the following resolution from the Afoore Parish Council : It having been reported to this Council that the District Council is in negotiation with the Runcorn Urban Authority to let them have the use of the small-pox hospital at Moore in case of an epidemic breaking out in Runcorn, desire to urge upon the District Council the advis- ability of arranging that all patients should be conveyed to the hospital witWout passing through the village of Moore and it was suggested that the Ship Canal forms the best, quickest and safest route. The resolution was rererred to the Isolation Hospital Committee. TIE_ RECENT OUTBREAK 01' ANTHRAX... . .

It was decided to approach the County Council with the object of having circulated amongst cattle owners in the district a pamphtet issued by the Board of Agri- culture on the diseases of animals. . -

Mr. Woodw-arCiTalithere—had--;ecently, in a neigh- bouring parish, been a case of anthrax. It seemed to him that if all cattle keepers had a copy of the pamphlet a similar occurrence could not happen, as the symptoms of the disease were so minutely andaccurately described as to be at once discovered. The Clerk reported that there was standing to the credit of Stockton Heath and Appleton some V 39 ss. 6d. invested in coneols, and he had obtained the sanction of the Public Works Loan Commissioners to use that sum for the reduction of the debt. It was decided to authorise the Treasurer to sell the consols, and to apply the proceeds as suggested. Mr. Linaker : What will we lose on the transfer ? The Clerk : Very little. The money was invested when consols were low.

div.head: ST HELENS.
div.p: ST HELENS.
ST. HELENS COLLIERY DISPUTE. A NEW AGREEMENT.

The representatives of the six or seven hundred men employed at what is known as the Bottom Pit,belonging to the St.Helens Colliery Company,on Wednesday met the management for the purpose of discussing an appeal made by the men for better terms. The men had asked for certain allowances for waggoning and extra work, and had gone so far as to decide by ballot to strike if ' their request .was not granted. The ballot showed a great majority in favoiv of handing in final notices on Tuesday, and the men were definitely prepared for a strike. Fortunately, Tuesday's meeting was success- ful in settling the differences, and we understand that it has been arranged for a new agreement to be drawn up and signed this week-end, uuder which the men will be granted certain increases of pay.

div.head: INCANDESCENT V. ELECTRIC LIGHT.
div.p: INCANDESCENT V. ELECTRIC LIGHT.

A deputation of St. Helens tradesmen waited upon the St. Helens Lighting Committee some time ago to ask that the main streets of the town should be more effectively . illuminated than by the arc lamps which have been in use for some time. The Electricity Com- mittee have reported on the matter to the Gas Com- mittee, and it has been decided to dispense with the are lamps and to fit a couple of powerful incandescent lamps to the tramway standards. It is claimed that this will cost £125 per annum, and be a saving of £9O on the present annual cost. THEFTS FROAI ST. HELENS PAWNSHOPS.

Richard Kerwick, a St. Helens loafer with a bad record, was convicted at St. Helens on Monday of stealing two jackets from the door of Mr. Westhead's pawnshop in Parr Stocks-road on Saturday at noon. Kerwick was seen taking the articles, and when he was followed by the shop assistant and Police-Constable Gleave he ran across some fields and pelted the officer with stones. He had just picked up two large stones when he was caught. Kerwick had been twenty-ninef times before the court (four times this year), and when he was sentenced to three months' haul labour he said he was sorry it was not mom—Joseph Kerfoot, another man, took a pair of 'trousers from the front of Mr. Grundy's pawnshop in Tontine-street on Saturday night, and went into a passage a few yards away and changed them for his old ones. The shop manager, Adam Rath- bone, went to him, and Kerfoot assaulted him.— Kerfoot was also sentenced ta three months' hard labour.

EARLESBOWN VIADUCT BAND. This band journeyed on Saturday to take part in the Crystal Palace competition, but they arrived so later as a result of the train service being affected by the fog that they were disqualified with several others.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

PASSIVE RESISTANCE. At Newton Petty Sessions last Thursday Mr. G. S King, Bridge-street, Earlestown, was again summoned for non-payment of his poor rate amounting to Lis. 10s. Gd.—Mr. King said it was all paid except the Education portion.—The usual order was made.—Mr. King was the only "passive resister " on this occasion but orders were also made on James Curran, William ; Bennett, and Kate Grimoldby, for unpaid poor rates,on the application of Mr. H. Houghton, assistant overseer. —Many other rate cases were settled without being called on.

div.head: MR. SEDDON M.P.'S CHALLENGE.
div.p: MR. SEDDON M.P.'S CHALLENGE.

Mr. J. A. Seddon, M.P. for the Newton Division,who recently spoke at a Labour demonstration in Burnley, writes as follows to Mr. Sparling, the secretary of the Burnley Trades Council :—" I note that the Rev. J. H. Robinson,secretary of thc Burnley Free Church Council, made the following statement :--` If they watched very narrowly the trend of Socialism it tended to be immoral in everything in the bigger and wider interpre- tation of the term.' If the latter part is not an ambigu- ous statement to cover retreat from a narrow, bigoted, cowardly position I publicly challenge the gentleman either by public debate or written statement to prove his assertion."

div.head: POACHER SENT TO GAOL.
div.p: POACHER SENT TO GAOL.

At the Wigan County Police Court on Monday, James Whittle of Haydock, was charged with the poaching on the Garswood estate.—Mr. W. Lees stated that on Friday night, Lord Gerard's head keeper, and his assist- ants, were in a portion of the park when they heard several men setting nets. It was rather foggy at the time, and the head keeper gave directions for the other men to place themselves in position. They then approached the men, and when the prisoner saw them he attempted to get away, but ran into the arms of the keepers. Whittle was convicted for a similar offence about seven years ago.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for a month with hard labour. THEFT FROM HAYDOCK ASYLUM. Patrick Hurley, of Ashton, was charged at Newton Petty Sessions last Thursday, with stealing a diamond breast pin, of the value of £2, the property of Dr. Street, at Haydock Lodge private asylum. Michel Campion, employed at Haydock Lodge, identified the pin produced.—Thomas Brown, pawnbroker, of Wigan, deposed to receiving the pin into pledge from the defendant, who said he bought it for £4 in Liverpool. Having dad notice that the pin had been lost, he taxed the defendant with having stolen it, and he admitted it. Witness gave him into custody.—ln answer to Mr. Knowles, who defended, he said he had known the defendant as a respectable man.—Defendant was sworn, and said he found the ring some weeks after it had been lost, and took it to two pawnbrokers in Wigan to ascertain the value of it. He knew the owner was likely soon to be discharged from the Asylum, and intended then to give it to him, but having found it in the airing court three weeks after it was lost he thought he would be suspected of stealing it if he had taken it to Dr. Street. He denied wanting to pown it,his object being to ascertain the value, which had been stated to be £7 10s. but he did not believe it was so much.—Mr. Knowles urged the defendant's statement on the Bomb, but the Chairrgan said they considered the case proved, and fined defendant 10s. and costs. EARLESTOWN CRICKET CLUB. AVERAGES—SEASON 1906.

The season of 1900 has been a memorable one in the annals of Earlestown cricket, local wielders of the willow having captured the chief honours in two strong competitions. The firstiwas the notable victory of August 11th in London, where, after having dis- posed of a strong Wolverton team in June,they defeated the metropolitan representatives of the L. & N.-W. Railway for the General Manager's Cup. The most meritorious success, however, was in winning the cup and medals of the West Lancashire League, which last year fell to Newton. Tnis was the result of good play and sound generalship all through the season. The first team played 19 matcbes (2 more than last year), won 13, lost 3, the other 3 being drawn. There were only 11 victories in 1905. The runs scored were 1,920 for the loss of 159 wickets, average 1207 as agairst 13.18 in the last season. The total score of the opposition was 1,095 for 177 wickets, average 7.57 as against 10.15 in 1905. J. Crawley, who heads the list with 10.21, compares unfavourably with W. H. Crowther's lead last year of 29.C4. In fact Crawley was second to Crowther then with 2081. George Marsh, who only played 3 innings last year, jumps from the eleventh to the second position with 15.91. closely followed by his brother, the team's captain, with 1561, who also made better flgufes last year. W. IL Crowther has seceded several points, as also has R. A. Robinson and J. H. Alderson. A.Wolfe played one innings only last year,but now comes into a very respectable position as a batsman. In bowling the veteran R. Bates is at the top again, as was the case last year, and with a slightly improved average for much heavier work, not less than 98 mor overs. Next comes J. H. Anderson, whose figures show a marked improvement, 17 more overs and 1013 per wicket as against 15•6 G. George Marsh, H. Warburton, and A. Wolfe also rendered valuable help in this depart- ment. A point well worthy of notice is the splendid wicket-keeping of G. B. Leigh. Ho coaght 15, stumped 18, and only allowed 37 byes during the whole season. BATTING.—FIRST Tai.

Warrington Rural District Council. The monthly meetirvr of the Warrington Rural District Council was held at Bewsey Chambers on Wednesday when there were present : Mr. Brooks (presiding), Dr. Murray, Messrs. G. Mather, W. Houghton, J. Backhouse, R. Forshaw, J. W. Knowles, J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), B. S. Newcombe (surveyor), 11. 11. Bnrnage (assistant surveyor), F. W. Kerfoot (inspector), and Dr. Sephton (medical officer.) The Clerk reported the receipt of a memorandum from the Cheltenham Rural District Council addressed to the Local Government ' Board with regard to the Motor Car Commission. Mr. Backhmse : We ought to record our protest against the finding of the Commission in abolishing the speed limit. Dr. Sephton reported that during the month there had been 24 births and 28 deaths. The death-rate was equal to 28 per 1,000 as against 20 the average of the past three months and 32 for the corresponding period of last, year. Sixteen of the deaths occurred at the County Asylum, excluding which tie death-rate for the district would be equal to 122 per 1,000. The report was an excellent one. Mr. Mather: It is the best we have had for some I time.

MAZAWATTEECOCOA.—BRIZC AND BONUS SCHEME.— The attention of our readers is called to the great prize and bonus scheme (advertised in another column) which the Mazawattee Co. have arranged for users of their [famous Red Label Cocoa. A coupon is enclosed in each tin sold, varying in value according to the size of the tin. A !first prize of £5O is offered for the largest number of coupons and there will also be a secoud prize of .£25 a third prize of £l5, a fourth prize of £lO, ten awards of £5 each, 100 of £1 each, and 200 of 10s, each, in order of merit. Presentation boxes of Mazawattee chocolates will be sent to those who prefer to collect coupons for that purpose only. Mazawattee Itpd Label Cocoa is of particularly fine and pure quality and is economical owing to its strength and richness.

A unique scene was witnessed at Hull on Thursday when a bridal party and the invited guests were con- veyed from the church in Corporation tramcars to St. George's Hall, where a reception was held. People in the streets watched the strange wedding conveyances with curiosity.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.

Services for Sunday. Bold-street Wesleyan Church: Preachers, 10.30, Rev. J. Gunnell; 6.30, Rev. J. Manning. Bewsey-road IVesleyan Church : Preacher, 10.30 and 6.30, Rev. E. Davidson, Connexional Evangelist. Golborne-street Baptist Church : Preacher, 10.30 and 6.30. Rev. F. Batten, Portsmouth. Latchford Baptist Church : Preasher, Rev. J. F Matthews. Subjects, 10.30, "Kingship by Suffering,' e.o, "The agony of a God-forsaken Christ." St. John's Presbyterian Church (Harvest Thanks- giving) : Preacher 10.30 and 6.30, Rev. J. L. Milne. Special music will be rendered by the choir.

St. Mary's Bells. Sunday will be a red letter day in connection with St. Mary's (R.C.) Church, Buttermarket-street, as it will witness the blessing of the bells which have recently been hung in the new tower. The ceremony will be per- formed at-6 p.m.by the Abbot of Ample forth who at 11 in the morning will also celebrate pontifical high mass. Both in the morning and evening a special sermon will be delivered by the Right Rev. T. 3. Cummins, 0.5.8.

Rev. R. If. Bowen's Farewell. The Rev. R. H. Bowen curate of St. Paul's Church, who has accepted the curacy of Holy Trinity, Darwen, preached his farewell sermon on Sunday morning, from the teat" That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith "—Eph. iii. 17. At the conclusion of his discourse, the rev, gentleman and that that was the last occasion on which he wonad address the congregation, and he therefore, wished to give them a wish and a warning. The wish should be the wish that Christ might dwell in their hearts by faith, but they must take warning that, if they did not ask God for the wish to be granted they would of all men be the most miserable, because without the faith of Christ there was no true and lasting happiness on earth. Mission at Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church. The Rev. Edward Davidson, connexional evangelist, is conducting a special ten days' mission at Bewsey- road Wesleyan Church. The mission has been prepared for by a thorough canvass of the neighbourhood, some 4,000 houses having been visited and letters of invita- tion distributed. Mr. Davidson met the workers on Saturday night and gave an address outlining his methods and spent some time in practis- ing new hymns from the Free Church Evangelist Hymn Book which is being used throughout the mission. On Sunday Mr. Davidson occupied the pulpit morning and evening and delivered powerful discourses which were listened to with marked attention. There was a very large congregation in the evening at a service of great interest. The singing was led by an augmented choir. Hr. IV. Pearce presided at the organ. The services have been continued during the week, and on Thursday afternoon there was a meet- ing for Bible reading. There have been good attend- ances and the mission promises to be a great success. Organ and Vocal Recital at Wycliffe Church. At Wycliffe Church on Monday evening a most enjoy- able organ and vocal recital was given by: Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac. and Mr. James Coleman, a member of the choir of Lichfield Cathedral. It was somewhat disappointing that owing to counter-attractions in the town and the heavy rain, the attendance was meagre. The programme submitted was an admirable one and both gentlemen are to be highly complimented upon the ability with which the various items were rendered. Mr. Payton played six pieces—" Schiller March" (Meyerbcer), Air (with variations) " Jerusalem the Golden" (Spark), "Question and Answer" (Wolsten- holme), "Barcarolle" (Sternitale Bennett). descriptive piece" Fantasia Pastorale" (Wely), and finally," Grand Offertoire in D" (Batiste). Each was given with taste and skill and served -to demonstrate the marked improve- ment which has been affected in the tone and power of the instrument. Mr. Coleman possesses a very fine baritone voice and gave four items—" The Sower went forth sowing " (Alan Malcolne), "0 God ! have mercy " (St. Paul, Menilchssolat), " Why do the nations " (Messiah, Handel), and " The Radiant morn " (a song of his own composition) with beautiful effect. The audience was delighted and in response to hearty applause Mr. Coleman repeated the latter stanza of his last song. A collection was taken on behalf of the Renovation Fund.

div.head: HARVEST FESTIVALS.
div.p: HARVEST FESTIVALS.

LEGH-ST. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHURCH. On Sunday last at the above church harvest thanks- giving services were held, when the Rev. F. Vaughan preached two splendid sermons to large congregations. In the afternoon a musical service was given, the title of the cantata being " David " and was exceedingly well rendered by the choir and friend 3 including the follow- ing soloists :—Miss Alice Bridge, Miss Alice Woodland, Miss Bessie Eckersley, Miss Eva Woodland, Mr. John Corrin, Mr. Warburton,Mr. E. H. Pearce, A.L.C.M., and Mr. George Gough, all the soloists being specially praiseworthy. The choir under the able conductor- ship of Mr. Spruce, rendered the choruses in a refined and effective manner. Miss Lily Fairhurst sang a solo with much taste at the evening service, and the choir : rendered the anthem" Sing unto the Lord "which was I sung with great effect. Mr. Fred Podrnore presided at the organ. On Monday evening a fruit banquet was held, Miss P. Cruikshank sang with taste "Oh Divine Redeemer " and "The Message," her sister accompanied. Speeches were given by the Rev. C. L. Stowe, Mr. Bissell and Mr. B. T. Parkes. The collec- tions were very satisfactory. BAPTIS E' CHURCH, WARRINGTON. The harvest festival in connection with the above church was held last Sunday. The day had been looked forward to on account of the visit pf the Rev. J. T. Schofield (of Taunton), of a former pastor, who is highly respected by church and people. The church, which had been decorated by a band of energetic and willing workers, comprising the ladies of the church, presented a very pretty appearance, which called forth high praise from the splendid congregations which assembled at each service.—Mr. Schofield preached appropriate sermons, and based his morning remarks upon the words "Precious seed brought forth by the sun " (Deut. 3c. 14v.), and showed that all fruit required labour, but after all labour the ripening sun, and spoke upon the spiritual lessons taught us in the natural world. The musical service in the afternoon was I presided over by Mr. Norman Balmford (of Dewsbury.) ' The Co-operative Glee party, Miss L. Pliuston and Miss Carrie Hastings took part in the service, and all rendered their selections in El most pleasing and creditable manner. The Chairman in his remarks spoke as to the pleasure it gave him to be at the church once more and to take part in the services and appalled to the young people to become members of it and help it all they could. At the evening service the church was packed, the preacher basing his remarks on " God's mercies— man's responsibilities," Romans xii. 1. He showed that harvest festivals were not of modern idea, but had come down the ages, as seen in the offering of Cain and Abel, and later in the Jewish festivals, being acknow- ledgements of God's mercies and goodness, and they ought to lead us to consecrate ourselves to Him. During the service Mr. Sam Hassell gave a solo and the young people the anthem " With Thankfulness." The flowers were sent to the Infirmary, the fruit, etc., being sold on the Tuesday evening and the services were brought to a fitting conclusion by a social evening on Thursday. The total proceeds of the services were , £l7 16s. 9d.

div.head: SECRETS OF NATURE.
div.p: THE SECRETS OF NATURE.
Modern Improvements on Ancient Methods of Doctoring.

There has crept into the medical art in these latter days a habit of reliance on mysterious drugs extracted from minerals, rock, stones and strange earths,extracts concocted from coal-tar, and poisons from all sorts of strange sources. But this reliance is rarely justified by results, for the common effect of such drugs is to patch up a patient for a time only to fall shortly into a deeper relapse. In olden days folks relied on simple extracts from homely herbs, and knew nothing either of the. myriad nervous ills people suffer from to-daft, or the still stranger methods of seeking cure. Bile Beans for Biliousness—the grandest of modern family medicines—owe their phenomenal and consistent success to the fact that they are compounded only of simple herbs and roots. In purely herbal remedies there is absolute safety, for they do not obstruct the organs of the body with mineral deposits, nor do they chafe and inflame the delicate internal tissaes by drastic% action. The action in the stomach of the herbal ingredients of Bile Beans is as unique as their origin is simple. Bile Beans contain extracts from certain valuable herbs and roots which assist the digestion and assimilation in a perfectly natural yet powerful manner. Some mineral remedies will for a time produce similar results but they accomplish it in an unnatural fashion—by forcing over-production of the gastric juices, with the inevitable result that, the glands are so weakened by overwork that they fail altogether. The herbal extracts in Bile Beans dissolve in the stomach with the food and pass through the whole length of the alimentary canal. They exert a healing influence on the stomach,liver,kidneys and bowels. The extracts are also absorbed naturally into the blood with the food-elements which support life. Through the blood Bile Beans convey this tonic, healing, soothing, and purifying influence to remote parts of the system. Some int their rd a my doctorsediea Ipractice,m ayreturn nh ce er b s ma nd o re simples" relyo n natural tonics and alteratives which leave no foreign deposits in the body, which do not flog worn-out organ? into over-activity or dose them into lethargy and us lessness. But wise people rely on Bile Beans ' ) Biliousness, a medicine which they have tried and proved. No home should be without Bile Beans for Biliousness, the safest, surest, and purest of family medicines. Bile Beans build up the run-down system. They are a tonic-alterative of exceptional value to the ailing housewife, the anemic daughter, and the weary breadwinner, because they are the medicine of dis- tinguished merit and as different as they are superior to common family drugs.

div.head: WARRINGTON APOLLO PRIZE MALE CHOIR.
div.p: WARRINGTON APOLLO PRIZE MALE CHOIR.
Successful Concert at the Parr Hall.

The Warrington musical season may be said to have opened on Monday evening when the annual concert promoted by the Apollo Prize Male Choir was held in the Parr Hall. It was pleasing to see such a large audience,for the excellence of the programme certainly merited that full measure of public support which is so encouraging to those who endeavour, to elevate musical taste. From small beginnings the choir has progressed remarkably and has been instrumental in discovering local talent of no mean order, arid of directing it into the right channels. The organization is now probably stronger than ever in its history, and the enthusiasm shows no sign of waning. Of course, the work of the choir figured largely in Monday's programme, and it is only due to the members to say that, under the able conductorship of Mr. H Berrey, their singing gave the greatest pleasure to the audience, whose appreciation was most marked. There is a fine volume of voices, nicely balanced, and the listeners could not fail to be impressed with the atten- tion to details of expression and the lack of anything mechanical. A spirited " Sailor's Chorus "(Dr. Parry) formed a capital opening item, and went with a delight- ful swing. Particularly pleasing were the part songs The Bridal Dance" (R. Strauss), " To Celia " (Lee WiLiarns), and "Dance of the gnomes" (McDowsll) and the chorus "Fleeting life" (Cornalius) which form the test pieces at the Blackpool Musical Festival where the choir compete to-day. We hope they may add another laurel to their already highly creditable record. Speaking generally, the part-songs are of a refreshingly light and sprightly character, yet with many intricacies which require much careful training to surmount. The interpretations of these part-songs and of the beautiful chorus did the cboir great credit and called forth warm applause. Responding to an encore, the touching "Soldier's Farewell "—a gem of harmonl—was given ' With great effect. The stirring dramatic chorus " Spartan Heroes" (Protheree) served to bring into action the full resources of the choir, and the solo was _ .

well sung by Mr. Arthur Greenough. Two charmin g part songs, "The Day's Farewell" (Neggler) and The Image of the Rose " (Reichardt) were treated with taste and expression, Mr. R. W. Cook being the soloist. One of the most enjoyable selections was the descriptive chorus—" The Village Blacksmith " (Dr. Parry)—and this splendid setting which brings out very strikingly the varying moods of the familiar poem was interpreted in a meritorious manner.. Mr. Dan Gittens was the soloist. The pro- I _
motets had been fortunate in securing the service; of several artistes whose individual items much enhanced
the pleasure.of the evening. Madame Rathbone is well

knoCvn to Warrington gatierings and she fully main- tained her reputation by her admirable renderings of The Swallows " (Cowen) and "Until to-morrow' ' (aim). She possesses a soprano voice of consider- able range and flexibility and did justice to each of the selected songs, being heartily re-called: . •

, Miss Annie Worsley (contralto) also gained her full quota of the audience's approval by her artistic and expressive4treatment of At the nich hour of night " and "Avenging and 'bright" (C. IT. Stanford)—short songs which impressed one by their somewhat wierd melodies and their marked contrast in styles—and the beautiful and pathetic composition "She wandered down the mountain side" (Ciog). The latter in particular was sung with ranch feeling and called forth an unmistakable request for another item which was responded to with the ever-popular" Allan Water." Mr. Goose Platt has a robust and powerful baritone voice which he used to the best advantage in" Honour bids me speed away " (Collier) and that quaint song" The old plaid shawl " (Haynes). His interpretations of each were in particularly happy vein and he too had the honour of a recall. In the duet" The Harbour Lights " the voices of Miss Worsley and Mr. Platt blended with pleasing effect. Mr. John Paley, the champion cornet soloist of the world, is a favourite with Warrington concert-goers and he had a cordial reception. He is a wonderfully clever player and in a variety of pieces evidenced his complet,4 command over the instrument and his musicianly taste. He held the audience spell- bound and was accorded several enthusiastic encores. The humorous part of the programme was in the capable hands or Mr. Lindon Wyatt, who has also previously appeared under the auspices of the Apollo Choir. By his entertaining sketches, smart songs, and amusing stories he created laughter loud and long and his hearers were quite loth to part with him. Two efficient accomnanists were found in Mr. E. Wilkes, A.L.C.M. and Master W. Pearse.

div.head: SOCIAL QUESTION AND ITS SOLUTION.
div.p: THE SOCIAL QUESTION AND ITS SOLUTION.
By Mr. Henry Whitham.

In the " Examiner " of August 18th Mr. W. R. ' Lester, M.A., had an article, the heading of which was something like the above. Inasmuch as the article ; referred to, and others that may appear, deals with ; the greatest of all present .day questions, viz., Socialism, it may be well to brush aside apathy and! indifference, and instead of drifting blindly into it, keep the eyes of our understanding wide open so that the goal reached may be a sure and safe one. On my first reading of the article I was persuaded that it must have been written a number of years ago,, or if not the writer had completely failed to under- stand what the Socialism of to-day is. On a second perusal I was quite persuaded that the whole article was a mere burlesque and would certainly not be accepted by any Socialist as a correct inter- pretation of what Socialism stands for. As my books are altogether out of my reach I cannot quote from any of the up-to-date writers on Socialism and can therefore put - forward only my own views on the matter. Mr. Lester says, " Competition in itself is the bug- bear of Socialism ",—without any qualification as to the kind of competition. This may be true in the sense that the Socialist writer or speaker is charitable enough to take it for granted that his audience has sufficient perception to see the kind of competition referred to, viz, that which is meant when we say, "each man for himself and the devil take the hind- most" or" everybody for his own pocket." As a mere fact it is not the Socialist that is crying out so much against competition and therefore deserves Mr. Lester's strictures, as it is the capitalist who is absolutely barring it out and is trying his level best to guard and fenca in what we know as the Trust and make one huge, monopoly of the world's commerce. The lines of commerce that are now under the complete control of the Standard Oil Co., and are altogether outside the comprehension of the man in the street,are not in any sense carried on according to what may .be called competitive laws ; they are, in a word, one huge monopoly and every method is adopted however criminal it may be, to shut off all competition. 'Seven men, of whom Rockefeller and J. P. Morgan are the most conspicuous, rule Wall-street, and con- trol almost the whole of the American railroad systems. When the full significance of this is understood it will be clear how little competition there is, and how much misery has been caused for these men to gain their object. And yet these men compete with each other, while striving their utmost to narrow the circle of individual railroad companies. Each one of them is now before the Courts charged with giving rebates to favourable firms, and so interfering with the laws of competition, such laws being, as I understand them, an open field and no favour. When Socialists are charged with looking at competition as a "bug-bear" it is implied that business men look upon it with favour. I would ask, is this so? Does the tailor, the grocer, or the dealer in shoes lilts to see his next door neighbour underselling him in the competitive struggle? A case in point occurs to me. A number of years ago, and possibly it is to day, it was the rule in England for all wire manufacturers to pay their drawers according to one general wage list. So long as this continued there was harmony between employer and employees. A firm in Warrington not satisfied with this arrangement sought to 'gain advantage by the , introduction of lovely woman into the mills as wire-drawers. It was no fault of the firm's that it did not succeed ; had it been successful, other manufacturers must in self defence, have followed the same course. Now, I ask, did either employer or employee lodk upon this kind of 'competition with favour, or was it not the " bugbear " again making it appearance as it had already done through all the cotton mills of Lancashire and -York- shire ? Moro recently, unfair competition again inter- fered with the serenity of the British wire trade. This time it was foreign, and it was real. A sweeping reduction in the wage schedule was offered to the men. A strike in resistance came about, causing great loss to employers and tradesmen, and much misery to workmen's families. The unfair, yet successful, and well-protected German wire manufacturers were pay- ing their workmen about a third of the weekly wage the British wire drawers were earning. Of course British methods had to be brought up to date, but a considerable amount of labour was piled on the work- man to enable him to earn a living wage. I 'think what I have so far said is quite sufficient to prove that there is a competition that is not only barbarous in its methods and results but will be positively ruinous as the open markets of the world decrease in number. Let us look at it still further and in another direction, before taking up the concrete position of the Socialist with regard to competition. Is it not true that there is moaning throughout the English speaking world, that we are degenerating? Whichever way we look we see the mere money grubber, intent only on pelf. 'Art and all literature are being sacrificed to this moloch. Neither the. painter, sculptor, nor writer ever turned out good work when the object was merely to keep the pot boiling. Michael Angelo's work was not done for pot boiling purposes, yet there was ' a competition that was laudable. Dante's work, like Milton's, being outside competition was of the best, and the pay of the worst. Our dear old friend Oliver Goldsmith did the best of work when free from his creditors, but the trashy "Animated Nature" came when the pot had to be kept boiling. Scott's best work was done at the time he was clear of the creditor. All our best scientific writing was, and is done by men wbo are clear of the capitalist class. The history of the inventors of the ,-past century is the monstrous story of their spoliation by the capitalists ; it is a long and melancholy roll of martyrs. The inventor, by the very fact of his genius, is condemned with his family to ruin and suffering. Turning to*the Church the state of things is still worse. When Mr. Gladstone disestablished the Irish Church the greatest obstacle he had to meet was the money question. To-day the careful student will find that all the wrangling in the House of Commons has for its basic incentive the one magic a ord —money. And yet, not only will the :Church have to be Disestablished, the educational system will have to be put on a purely secular basis, but the cost feature will have to be entirely eliminated. I think I have scarcely missed one issue of "The Christian World," London, during the past twenty years, and I can truly say that the reading has done as much as anything else to canfirm me in my views as to the line of thought ;that was honest and true. There has recently appeared a series of ess43 written by one whom I consider the most forceful essayist in the world of letters to-day. Commencing with June 28th and continuing through about a dozen issues, the writer, the Rev. J. Brierly, has given to the world at the small cost of Is. such information as I heartily wish at least all my readers will try to get hold of. He says: " Where then does our Socialism come in? The mention of the French peasant proprietors supplies us with an answer. The true Socialism proposes not the extinction of property but its universal diffusion. We would give every man his joy of individual posses- sion." He further says : " John Morley has said, It is one of the discouragements of the student of history that he finds ideas uttered one of two or twenty centuries ago which are just as useful and just as little heeded now as they were when they were uttered." Going further "J. 8. says: "The message of the Primitive Church, the utterances of the Fathers, the " Republic" of a Plato, the " Utopia" of a More, the economic and social schemes of a Prondhou and a Saint Simon make, taken together, a very curious medley of reading. And yet these seemingly discordant voices are actually sounding one note. You can boil down their systems into a word. They all preach Socialism." " J. 13." in supping up says:— :' The task of the modern State is to replete the Iprinciple of public and private ownership so as to , secure the highest welfare of the individual and the ' community." I shall return to a part of the above quotation. I now wish to point out the utter impos- sibility of securing the highest welfare of the individual and the community under our present economic conditipns. In the Established Church Ai have at the top one who receives his thousaads of pounds a year. As the follower of One who had not where to lay His head, he may be a good man, but he is not true to his Master. Going down the line, and taking the poor Curate along with us, we meet with the fox-hunting Rector, and if we have read " Yeast "we shall know something of a life in a village. I have somewhere a long list of the manner in which these church dignitaries, who, in vain repetition, say " Lead us not into temptation" invest their money. It is just horrible to me that these men should call themselves Christians. Why, I would raffish ten thousand times over take my chances of the future than he linked with these men. iThe list I refer to shows the immense amount of

div.head: I money the chnrch kas invested in the liquor traffic, and apropos of this I cut the following out of to-day's
div.p: I money the chnrch kas invested in the liquor traffic, and apropos of this I cut the following out of to-day's

LONDON, August 25th.—One of the anomalies of the established Church of England is that, like the Trinity Church estate in New York, it owns vast property in London and Lancashire, of which the principle tenants are saloon keepers. Recently the Church of England Estate Com- missioners were requested to publish details of their saloon property in London. Reluctant to make public the amount of church revenue from the liquor troffic, they refused to do so. It is known however, that there are fifty-seven saloons on the church's Lancashire„property, and there must be many more in London. • Doubtless action will be taken in Parliament, which created the Estates Commission,to force the church officials to give the desired information. The taxpayers think themselves entitled to know the details of the church's revenue, as they con- tribute 10,000,000d015. of it annually in tithe tax. I remember a couple of instances of clerical doings that occurred some years ago. One was the strike of the London match-box makers, and the other was the doings of the Bible Socibty in the way of pro- ducing cheap Bibles. The chief characters in each of these lines of -tragedy were men who thought they belielk,d the Master when He said "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these, my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Now I ask, in all seriousness, is it not time that a complete clearance should be made of the present economic conditions? The money spent and that has first to be earned by the workers, brain and brawn, might as well be thrown into the sea, we should know then that it was working injury to none. As it is we are working in a vicious circle. Years ago "Alton Locke," and" Cheap clothes and nasty "were written. George Eliot gave us "Felix Holt." Hood gave us " The song of the shirt," and yet the con- ditions change not. Yob say Socialism is Utopian, but the present system is simply criminal to the last degree. President Schurman of Cornell University says: "To get and to have is the motto not only of the market, but of the altar and the hearth.' President Hadley of Yale University says: "If it were true that a man's success is measured by the money and the offices which he can command, or that the test of a good education is to be found in the fact that it fits a man to make money and get offices, the American would fast approach this end." One More illustration of the innate, rottenness of the economic conditions we have so jealously fostered. In all the stories I have read, the following irlipressed me most with the utter impossibility of resisting the lure of gold. George Whitefield was celebrated as the most eloquent preacher' of his day. Thilough the influence of Charles Wesley he. came to the States. His eloquence swept the country. In 1738 he founded in Georgia a home for the care of orphan children. This home was planned by Charles Wesley. At this time slavery was not per- mitted in Georgia, but it was not prohibited in the adjoining Carolinas Whitefield's early work was vehement denunciation of slavery. Listen to these words, " God is the same to-day as he was yesterday, and will continue the same forever. He does not reject the prayers of the poor and destitute nor dis- regard the cry of the meanest negro. Their blood I which has been spilt these many years, in your 'respective provinces, will ascend up to heaven against you." Now comes in the economic condition. It took money to run his orphanage, and it took him all his time to keep it on its feet. There were no Rocke- fellers in those dap. Still there was a short cut and a legal way to get money without work, if one's con- science could be made sufficiently plastic. Recently we have seen some dallying and fumbling about taking Rockefeller's millions. The Rev. George White- field knew how to manage this liitle matter. History tells us he said : "I wonder the negroes have not more frequently risen up in arms against their owners, and though I heartily pray God they may never be per- mitted to gain the upper hand, yet should such a thing be permitted by Providence, all good men must acknowledge the judgment would be just." The Historian says : Whitefield discovered what clear gain it was to rob the poor of their wages, how safe and expedient a thing to do if the law would sanction it; how much easier to sup/39ft these pier orphans the constant theme of his eloquence —if there was nothing to pay for the labour on which they depended." Hildreth's history says : " Even Whitefield and Habersharn, forgetful of their former scruples strenuously pleaded with the trustees of Georgia in favour of slavery under the old pretence of propitiating in that way the Christian religion. Habersham wrote :—" Many of the poor slaves in America have already been free men of the heavenly Jerusalem." The Christian said to these would-be-slave-owners who were short of money "IS I you take slaves in faith and with intent of conducting them to Christ, the action will not be a sin, but may prove a benediction." Thus as usual, the religious sentiment was , made the tool of avarice for the enslavement of mankind.

Am I not right in saying that, if the present economic system is t') be maintained, if we are ta carry it along with us into the near future, when we shall grapple in our own markets with the cheap labour of the Asiatic, then such civilization as we have is doomed.
I. ViTHITHA/M.
Alameda, California, September 15th, 1906. , (To be continued.)

div.head: Records Broken at Warrington.
div.p: Records Broken at Warrington.

The excellent programme at the annual gala of the Warrington Swimming Club attracted a crowded attend- ance at the Legh-street Baths on Tuesday evening, and those present had the satisfaction of witnessing two successful attacks upon existing records. or the first time the 100 yards Liverpool and District Ladies Championship was decided at Warridgton, and interest in the event was increased by the appearance of Miss D. Curwin, Prima Dolphin S.C., who tied with Miss M. Scott in 190 in creating a record for the distance. Miss Curwen made a good start and swimming strongly quickly placed the issue of the race beyond doubt. The winning of the gold medal was not, however, her only triumph, as her time being returned at 1 min. 23 34 Isees., she has established a new record, the previous fastest time being 1 min. 24 3-5 secs. The other record which was broken was that for the local 150 yards open championship of Warrington. When this competition for the Licensed Victuallers' Perpetual Challenge trophy was decided in 1897 T. Locker covered the distsnce in 11 min. 29 secs, and until Tuesday night his time was a record. Pemberton and R. Allen (holder) were both favourites for the race but the first-named displayed the best form and finished first in 1 min. 54 secs.

The Schoolboy Championship of Warrington and District, for the Thornton challenge shield and methls resulted in a good race. R. Atkinson was placed first with H. Harding second, and P. Chalmers third. The Works Squadron contest for the Sir Gilbert Greenell challenge and gold medals, with gold centre medals for the runners up, aroused great interest. The finalists were P. and K, and Monks Hall and from the start P. and K. took the lead and succeeded in main- taining it until the end, winning by several yards. There were ten entries in the local 50 yards ladies' handicap, for a ladies' dressing case or a gold bangle (presented by the Mayoresss) ; a button book and shoe lift in case ; and a ladies' companion. The heat winners were :—A. Collins, 13 ; A. Bennie, 18 ; M. Barlow, scratch, and S. Davenport 22. After a good race Miss Bennie carried off the first prize with Miss Collins second and Miss Ihrlow third. - -

The Warrington Post Office were not able to put a strong team in the water against Liverpool Post Office with the result that the Liverpudlians won, by half-a- length, the silver medals offered, Forty-two competitors entered for the 50 Yards Junior Handicap, the winners of which were :-1, M. Aukland ; 2, H. Partridge; 5, H. Stirrup ; 4, J. Sutton. In the 100 yards local handicap the seniors had little chance to shine against the junior competitors they being too heavily handicapped. The race resulted in a win for A. Isherwood, with C. Woods second and R. Beaman third.. A boys water polo match between Warrington and St. Helens proved an interesting and exciting affair, and resulted in a'victory for St.Helens by five goals and two. The St. Helens lad thoroughly deserved their victory being much quicker on the ball. At the conclusion of the gala the prizes were pre- dented by the Mayoress (Mrs. Bolton.) During the evening Mr. Blowcock was presented with the Swimming Cinb's gold medal fo; a gallant attempt to rescue a man from drowning at Latchford. The facts, which we recorded at the time, were that Mr. Bowcock gallantly went into the Ship Canal and succeeded in rescuing a man who had jumped into the water, though, unfortunately, not before life was extinct. Atkinson's Cafe's Ltd. (Golborne-street and Bridge- street) kindly gave refreshments to the competitors.

I Thomas White, of 9, York-street, Oldham, fell from the upper portion of the offices of the White Star Line- in James-street, Liverpool, and was killed. He was one of the best known steeplejacks in Oldham, and was 36 years of age.

div.head: INDEMNIFYING THE MAYOR.
div.p: INDEMNIFYING THE MAYOR.
MORE ABOUT THE EDELSTEN ACTION.

opinion no action could be against the Mayor. It was an absurdity to think-- The MAAOE : Why do you refuse the indemnity? Councillor PEMBERTON : For the reason that the Corporation would weaken its position when it says "We won't carry out the agreement because we have not been parties to it" and then turns round and indemnifies you. It is playing a double game. It is a ridiculous position to take up. The MAYOR: I think the position is ridiculous all round.

Councillor NIMBERTON : I agree. There is not the slightest doubt, in my mind, that the man who ought to stand the brunt of this is the Town Clerk. He is the legal adviser of the Corporation' he knows what the Municipal Corporations Act is and he knows this ought to have been passed.

The MAYOR: Do you mean to tell me the Corpora- tion is liable for the actions of its servants ? Councillor PEMBERTON said "no," for the reason that the Municipal Corporations Act clearly laid it down that no act of any committee oeservant was complete without having received the sanction of the Council.

Councillor PEMBERTON then objected to the Town Clerk talking to the Mayor. The MAYOR observed that the To*n Clerk had told him that he thought Councillor Pemberton wait wrong. Councillor PEMBERTON: I have no doubt he will tell you lam wrong. He is considering his position. The TOWN CLERK You are not responsible for my position. Councillor PEMBERTON: And the Council is not going to be responsible if I can help it. This is one of the most serious cases we have had.
The MAYOR : Go on. WeinWe—liad them every day. They are all serious. Commillor PEMBERTON You will have to borrow money for this—

The MANOR: Do you think threats bother me? Cobncillor PemeaaroN lam not making threats. We have been charged with not being straightforward, so I will tell you what course we are going to adopt. Continuing, he said the Council would have to go to the Local Government Board for power to borrow the money for this. The Local Government Board would be no party to any illegal transaction, and would not grant the loan. The result would be that the money would have to come out of the rates in one year. In his opinion if this indemnity was not passed the whole case would fall to the ground. The whole thing was a question of bluff, in his opinion. Their opponents had not a hundred thousand to one chance. As soon as Counsel got up and mentioned that this had not received the seal of_the Council the case would drop against the Council. Supposing the case went on against the Mayor. He would have to say he signed the agreement on the advidie of the Town Clerk, and there was not the slightest doubt to his (Councillor Pemberton's) mind that the Town Clerk was the responsible man. Time after time they (the Non-Traders) had fought against secrecy of committees, and time after time they bad been promised it would not occur again. Hare was a case involving £B,OOO and the members of the Council, outside a few on the committee, had not the option of saving whether they would purchase the property or not. Not a single member of the committee said the agreement was in accordance with what they agreed with Mr. Edelsten. No agreement should be signed I until it was submitted to the committee which had authorised it. Not a single member of the Council knew what the agreement was before it was signed. That was a disgraceful and dangerous state of things. Were they going to allow. this sort of thing to go on? He appealed to those who represented the ratepayers to stop it. If they indemnified the Mayor, and the case against the Corporation fell through, the judge might go against the Mayor as he would not have to suffer,and in the interest of the ratepayers he (Coun- cillor Pemberton) asked the Cowneil to say it would be a mistake to give an indemnity. They had to fight for the benefit of the ratepayers, irrespective of anyone's interests—the Mayor's, Ole Town Clerk's, or anyone else's. What they would do afterwards, if•the Atlayor really had to pay, was another question. ' The Tows CLERK: lam sure you don't expect me to reply to the observations of Councillor Pemberton, but—

Councillor Pminstrros : I object to the Town Clerk speaking. He has no right to make a statement. The Town Clerk resumed Ms seat. Councillor STOTT prefaced his speech with the remark that he was thetb to represent the ratepayers. The MAYOR: Only one man represents the rate- payers. (Laughter). Councillor STOTT : Then I must be the one .( Loud Laughter). Continuing he said the Council had adopted this custom for a very long time in regard to the pur- shase of property. Some months ago, on the motion of Councillor Pemberton, they unanimously passed a resolution which would prevent anything of that character occurring again, and seeing that this action was done previous to that alteration being carried he thought it would be very unfair indeed if the members of the Council tried to saddle what might be a very large expenditure upon the Mayor, who had only been actingaccording to the custom on behalf of the Council. (Hear' hear.) He honestly believed the Mayor and other Mayors had acted similarly in the past without their actions having been questioned. He did not say It was a wise thing for the Mayor to do, but bethought he was acting in the interest of the Council and the ratepayers and it would be absolutely mean if they refused the idemnity and so saddled a large expense upon their agent, though he (the speaker) regretted as much as anybody what the Mayor had done on the advice of the Town Clerk. They had bees told that those who had voted for the indemnification might be surcharged with the cost. Well, he supposed they would have to stand their corner. He was afraid, so far as he was concernel, it would be a very small opruer— (laughter)—but still he was prepared to face the threats in a case of this character. (Hear, hear.) He believed that such a lesson would have been taught them by the difficult position in which they had now been placed, that not only future Mayors, but the chief officials of the town would not be likely to allow such a difficulty to a rise again. (Hear, hear.) Councillor PEIII3ItEtToN : It has not been the custom to pass these things. A great many purchases have come before the Council.

Councillor MAGINN said no one condemned the pur- chase of the property more than he did. The position of Mayor in a town like Warrington, where no allow- ance was granted from the rates, was no sinecure. If at the end of three years' service they were going to mulct the Mayor in costs it would be a very poor return indeed, and he was afraid that in future the town would have to go " Nfayor-hunting." He believed the Corpora- tion had a good clue, but what they were asked to do was to indemnify the Mayor, whatever they might think' of the mistake he made by signing the agreement as William Bolton, brewer, and not Mayor. A similar mis- take might have been made by anyone who happened to be in the hapny position of being a brewer. (Laughter.) The Mayor did not stand to gain a penny by the trans- action, so far as be knew ; otherwise he would have left him to hang 115, his own rope. Alderman BENNETT thought Councillor Pemi)erton was wrong in discussing the case, as it was sub judice. He could not conceive of anything more intolerable than that the Council should repudiate acts done in their behalf and in good faith by the head of the Council. It would make the position impossible. If the Mayor spent all his waking hours and sleeping hours too at the Town Hall he could not go into matters in complete detail ' and he must be in the hands of the officials to some extent. _

Councillor PF,MBERTON : The officials should treat him right. (Cries of " Order.") Alderman BENNETT : lam not going to follow you in a veiled attack on Mr. Whittle. Continuing he said that in private life the man who would repudiate an obligation of this kind would not be worthy of the name of man and the Councillors who would repudiate the Mayor and leave him in the lurch on such a question would not be worthy of the name of good citizens. Continuing. Alderman Bennett said he objected to the calm presumption of a section of the Council that they were the only people who had the interests of the ratepayers at heart. Service of the ratepayers, he held, was not purely a matter of £ s. d. and the amount of the rates. If that was their idea it would be possible to adopt \ a palicy which would practically reduce the rates to zero. The effect, how- ever, would be to make the town a howling wilderness, a disgrace to civilization, and an inferno, instead of a place fit for civilized people to live in. He contended that during the period he had been associated with the Council the policy pursued had been dictated by a sincere desire to promote the interests of the ratepayers from the highest standpoint.

div.head: Lively Council Discussion.
div.p: Lively Council Discussion.

One of the most important subjects under discussion at the meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday evening was the granting of an indemnity to the Mayor, who has been included as a defendant in the Edelsten action,re the purchase of the Mersey Works. The General Purposes Committee reported that a letter was read from Mr. Josiah Longland, asking the Corporation for their formal indemnity to Mr. William Bolton (the Mayor) as one of the defendants in the action commenced by Col. Edelsten against the Corpor- ation and himself, against all damages, costs and expenses, and any order which may be made against him in the action or in relation thereto." It was resolved "That an indemnity in the terms of Mr. Lo*land's letter be granted to Mr. William Boltonyani that the common seal be affixed thereto."

The Tows Cutax reported to the General Purposes Committee that he had taken out a summons to strike out the alternative claim in the statement of claim in the action of Edelsten v. The Corporation and Bolton. The MAYOR moved, and Alderman PaIa:COMB seconded the adoption of these minutes. Councillor WILDING moved an amendment that the resolution be not confirmed. He said his reason for doing so was that they, as a Council, had no authority either on moral or legal grounds, to indemnify a third party at the expense of the. ratepayers. Councillor CIINNINGTON seconded. Councillor CRANTLER. asked the Ma7or if he knew when he signed the agreement that it had not the sanction of the Council.

The lkleyort replied that he had signed eight or nine documents that were brought before him that day, and he was continually signing them. Councillor CHANTLER said in this case it turned out a responsible document. Did the Mayor sign it ivithout looking at it ? . . . . .

The MAYOR : I have to take it on the authority of the officials that it must be in order. I don't bother with red tape. lam not a lawyer. Councillor CHANTLER said it placed members of the Council who wished to vote straight in a funny position. Th 9 MAYOR explained that the indemnification of himself meant this. No man could serve two masters. The Council was served with a lwrit for performance. He (the Mayor) was also served with a writ. if he was to help the Council he must have an indemnity; if not, he wasto look after himself. " You want me to help the Corporation," continued the Mayor, " and my solicitor says I ought to have an indemnity." Councillor STorr asked the Town Clerk if it was legal to indemnify the Mayor. The TOWN CLERK: In my opinion the High Court would say the Council is quite justified in giving an indemnity to the Mayor. Councillor DICKENSON asked the Town Clerk whether he knew when he asked the Mayor to sign the document that it was illegal. (Laughter.) The MAYOR : He (the Town Clerk) simply brought it to me and said the Street improvement Committee had made a bargain with Mr. Edelsten, and someone in authority ought to sign it on their behalf, and I signed it. _

Councillor DICKENSON said that considering they paid the Town Clerk £7OO a year he thought the Town Clerk ought to look after the ratepayers' interests. The TOWN CLERK: Which I always have. Councillor DIcKaNsON : Not in this case. (Cries of " Order.") The MAYOR: The only mistake they made was that they did not ask Alderman Bennett, but they did Rot think he was as much an authority as I was. (Laughter.) Councillor WRIGHT : I ask if the Council to-night agrees to this indemnity to you as Mayor does it bind the Council to the agreement? The Tows CLERK : No sir. The MAYOR: No, it only makes me join with the Corporation in this action. Councillor LORD said that, supposing, if they indemnified the Mayor against everything, a burgess took the matter to court to set aside the payment, what would be the position of councillors who voted for the indemnity, if the payment was disallowed? He had reason to believe that such action would be taken„and he wanted to know whether Councillors who supported the proposal would be surcharged. • The TOWN CLERK: I have already expressed my opinion that the High Court will, uphold the Corpora- tion in granting this indemnity. Councillor PEMBERTON supported the amendment. He said the resolution was very sweeping. It said that they should indemnify the Mayor against all damages, costs, and expenses. It amounted to this—that if the Court found the Mayor was liable the Council would have to pay all the Mayor's costs and the Corporation's Costs. _

The 11A von.. You cannot discuss possibilities and Probabilities. Councillor PEIMBEEtTON : I am discussing the Opinions readehers. The Mavou : I think I should leave it, as you are only showing your hand in the event of an action. CollaCillOr PENIBERTON : Oh, no, I am not.—Con- tinning, he said he would warn the Council that he was advised this was illegal. The Council might incur the expense but steps would be taken to ask the Court that the ratepayers should not pay it. If they passed the resolution, it would weaken the Conncil's position in the action. The Council had denied their liability on the ground that the agreement had not received the seal of the Corporation, and also that it had not received the consent of the Council. In the opinion of Counsel those two points were fatal and no action could be against the Corporation. In his(Councillor Pemberton's)
