There was the best crowd in an ordinary League match at Broughton that there has been for a long time. Quite 12,000 people lined the enclosure—an indication that the new rules are producing football which interests the average spectator, and that War- rington are 'ovular visitors. Saturday's game was, however, a disappointment to many. From the out- set it was nothing but a punting and marking duel with an occasionel forward burst and some erratic attempts at passing. For two teams of the reputation of Warrington and the Rangers the exhibition was pitiable. They showed how the game should not be played insteaa of developing the finer points for the delectatidn of the public. It was really amazing at times to see the way in which the backs punted, and kicked and punted again for all they were worth. Many of the spectators must have gone home with stiff necks through watching the ball,, Blb Wilson was the worst offender of the lot and a chance visitor to the ground would never have imagined that he was the crack Centre of he Northern Union firmament.

This punting is getting into a disease —a veritable infectious plague, and club coaimitteea need to realise that it will soon reduce the game to a worse state than it was in before the alteration of the rules. With such methods in vogue as were resorted to on Satur- day the game is not Rugby football at all but a hotch- potch of the two codes and a bit of ballooning thrown in. Unfortunately some clubs—perhaps most —are indifferent to the kind of football so long as their own team is winning matches. But it has to be continu- ally borne in mind that the Northern Union is fight- ing for its life this season, and if the game is not attractive it will soon bring about theidownfall of the Union and the clubs comprising it. I was very sorry to read that Bradford's severe defeat of Salford on Saturday was due to their abandoning half and three- quarter combination for kick and rush methods. The lesson is supnosed to have been taught them the week previous by Hunslet. But what a fallacious idea the Park Avenue authorities must have got hold of. See what fate has befallen the teachers of the lesson, Hunslet. They can kick with perhaps more effect than any team in the League, but on Saturday the tactics which had won them every match were completely put out of court by Wigan's brilliant combination and speedy running. Nothing has pleased me more in this season's football, and I hope the kick and rush brigades will soon see the error of their ways.

I should not like to include either Warrington or Broughton among the number but on Saturday they deserved to be placed in such a category. Broughton set the silly example and Warrington slavishly followed it. There were a few attempts at passing principally by Warrington, in the first half, but the halves were weak and nothing came of it. Even Sam James op the other side forsook his old and famous methods for the punt, yet there is more scope to-day for good combination than ever. James,Wilson, and Hogg ilI be no more a terror to opponents if they keep on kicking. Warrington stood their ground pretty well and at half-time the score was two points each, but really the home side should have got the lead but forluingling. In the second half they beat Warrington for possession and had the most of the play. though several raids by Brooks, Taylor and Fish came near success. Harris's wonderful goal- kicking settled the issue, but he was indebted to some reckless play by the Warrington forwards for nearly all his opportunities. The front rank men were too eager to play their proper game, and there was little honest scrummaging on our side. There will have to be a change in method or some vacancies for aspiring juniors who know what a forward in a scrum is expected to do and that is push ! --- What little satisfaction there was in the match for Warrington came from the display of Berry and Brooks. By the way, the "B's " have always been among Warrington's best. Bate, Berry, 'Barber, Burton, Broady, Boscow, of the old brigade, occur to the memory at a moment's thought. Berry played very safely and stylishly at full-back • and methought

div.head: FATAL INSOMNIA.
div.p: FATAL INSOMNIA.

I The Widnes police report the death of Griffith Edward Davies, aged forty-seven, of 136, Albert-road, Widnes. At G. 15 on Sunday evening deceased left his mother and sisters in the parlour and went into the bathroom, where he inflicted shocking injuries to his throat. Davies was formerly a draughtsman at Widnes Gasworks, hut through nervousness he has not been able of late to follow his employment. During the last two weeks he had complained of want of sleep.

s he was qualifying for County honours. Brooks ball all the dash of the team practically, and had Fish thrown himself into the fray with equal energy Ile would have done better service. Brooks follows UP well and steadily. Fish prefers to look on when beer someone else has kicked. That's the difference between keenness and indifference. Warrington chief weakness was at half-back where J Davies No; practically useless as Hockenhall's deputy. TY others played fairly well behind a beaten paA' Barlow made a good impression at full-back fer Broughton, and the backs were all expert at fieldiui and kick, but Hogg played the best football. Forwar' they were very strong in both open and close work' The Broughtcrn forwards have to play for their placo each week and that makes a lot of difference. - Salford won at Warrington last year by 5 points to 4, a performance they should not be allowed to repeat to-day, especially as Lomas will be away assisting Cumberland. I think his absence is more serious for his side than that of Hockenhall, for Salford without Lomas are generally like a ship without a rudder. Warrington are sufficiently handicapped by the absence of the County half-back and Naylor, for reserves at the base of the scrum are scarce this season. DiVies is out of the question, so Jordan has been provisionally selected, but ttere is a possibility of Lambert turning out if his knee is sound enough.

It wso a keen game, and as a result of losing their tempers Harris (Warrington), and Bailey (Broughton), were sent off the field. A period of suspension doubtles° awaits both men. To-day the champions journey 0, Salford with rather Weakened forces but they should just about win. Stockton Heath Rugby Unionists are still showing 8/ good form,and it was a creditable performance of their's to draw at New Brighton on Saturday. A report a the match appears elsewhere. For the visitort Sampson at full back played a good game, his tacklin in particular being fine although his fielding was 14 times faulty. The threequarters as a whole were good and combined well but their efforts were nal' fled by the vigorous play of the New Brighton forwards; Gerard was the pick of the line, his try being a good ind.vidual effort. Langley at centre also plaY7t well. The halves were moderate. 11. Davenec played well and at times opened- the game 0127 1 good style. Ferguson made many good openings uu" spoiled them by bad transfers. The forwards vi.ll° were a man short the whole game, one man bacil3g missed the train,played a good game and in the second half more than held the heavier New Brighton R al aa • In the loose they were not quite the equs of the home eight. Gibbs, Smith and Gooke were the pick. 1 For New Brighton the forwards were the mainstay of the team and played a fine game, although they tired somewhat in the second half. 'The backs were not good with the exception of Tomes who repeatedly saved his side and was always dangerous when attacking.
The second team made short work of New Brighton B. at Stockton Heath, and won by 26 points to nil.

div.head: WARRINGTON'S FIRST*DEFEAT.
div.p: WARRINGTON'S FIRST*DEFEAT.

Warrington sustained their first defeat of the season on Saturday at Broughton where a fine crowd of 12,000 witnessed the Rangers triumph. Unfortunately for Warrington they had to find substitutes for Isherwood. Hockenhall, and Naylor, while Broughton were at full strength. Teams:— Broughton Rangers—Barlow, back; Hogg, Wilson, C. James and Harcis' three-quarter backs; S. James and Woodward, half-backs; Oram, Beetham, Darliston, Clempitt, Motham and Ruddick, forwards. Warrington—Berry, back; 'Wish Dickenson, I. Taylor, and Brooks, three-quarter backs; Davies and Lees, bait-backs; Preston, Swift, Boardman, Thomas, Harman and Heath, forwards. Referee, Mr. Bdmondson, Bradford ; touch judges, Messrs. J. Edwards, St. Helens, and E. Pearson, Leigh. Orem started the game and a long series of punting exchanges was the first • item of note, followed by penalties on both sides for off-side forward play. Warrington got in a round of passing which nearly ended in a score to Fish, but more kieking changed the venue and Barris gave Broughton the lead with a penalty goal. Warrington played with great dash on resuming and Taylor marking very cleverly in front of the home goal, Fish equalised the scores. Play was fast and furious after this but not very scientific. Broughton got over, but the forward pass NVLIA so palpable that a scrummage was ordered. Fish changed the scene by picking ' up on the line, rounding Hogg, and racing three parts the length of the field. The respite was only momentary and the Rangers should soon have been ahead, for a passing run left the Warrington line at the mercy of Wilson and C. James but the latter fumbled and, J. Davies saved on the line. Warrington responded strongly, Brooks and the forwards shining in some fast following up. Thomas made a dash for the line and passed. to Heath who was hurt and retired for a few minutes to the touch-line. Warrington still kept the Rangers penned in their own quarter and Fish missed a certain try through being out of plane when the ball was kicked across. Half-time Warrington 2 points; Broughton Rangers 2 points. On restarting, the home team was first to attack and Harris missed a nice pass with only a yard to go. There was a scrummage on the line and the same player made amendswith a try at the corner from a pass by Wood - ward. Harris failed at goal, but shortly after he placed three goals, one from a mark and two from penalties, so that Warrington were left a long way in arrears. They held their own fairly well in open play, but were seldom dangerous, though Brooks tried hard to get through the mangers' defence. Final: Broughton Rangers 4 goals 1 try (11 points) ; Warrington 1 goal (2 points).

RUNCORN r. SWINTON. Played at RuneOrn, before 2,000 spectators. 'Runcorn at once assumed the offensive, and in the first, two minutes Richardson placed a goal from a free kick. Runcorn were twice penalised, but Dixon and Oldfleld each failed wish the goal kick. Runcorn then attacked strongly, and Gartrell was forced over his own line, where be lost possession, Padbury scoring. Jolley failed to improve. Resuming, Hobson placed a fine penalty goal for Swinton. A grand round of passing between Jolley, Moran, and Deakin ended in the latter scoring, Jolley adding a goal. Booth and Garside broke away several times, but were unable to make much head- way, and a rush by the homefforwards placed the Swinton line in danger. From a scramble near the posts the ball was kicked to Deakin, who got possession, and rushing between the posts scored, Jolley adding a goal. Half-time score :—Runcorn 3 goals and 3 tries (15 points), Swinton 1 goal (2 points). After the interval the visitors were forced to defend and eventually a fine round of passing, in which Jolley, Flanaghan, and Deakin took part, ended in the latter scoring. Richardson failed at goal. From a penalty kick Jolley struck the upright, the ball rebounding into play again. Swinton were hard pressed, and Jolley and Deakin required a great deal of watching by the Swinton backs. Just before the finish Jolley completed the scoring with a dropped goal, and the result was : Runcorn,4 goals and 4 tries (20 points), Swinton 1 goal (2 points). Teams : Runcorn—Barrison, back ; Deakin, Richardson, Moran, and Flanaghan, threequarter backs ; Jolley and Watton, half backs; Walker,Williams, Padbury, Dobson, Kennedy, and Dixon, forwards. Swinton —Oldfleld, back ; Gartrell, Dixon, William- son, and Wallwork, threeparter backs ; Booth and Garside, half backs ; Cheetham, Davies, Pomfret, Hobson, Simister, and Barnett, forwards. WIDNES v. ST. HELENS.

Played at Widnes,before 2,000 spectators. The whole ! of the first half was fast and exciting, both teams play- ing the kick and rush game. Early on, from a forward rush, Winter had a glorious chance, but he was collared by Tilley. Towards the interval Widnes attacked, but try as they would they could not get over. Tilley failed at a placr-kick, and Taylor had a drop at goal,the ball just sailing under the bar, and half-time arrived with 00 score. Early in the second half Bococa gclll possession and gave to Manchester, who beat Tilley and scored. Oreevy failed at the goal kick. Shortly afterwards Widnes attacked, and after a round of pass- , ing Barker had a try at his mercy. He was 3bstructed. however, before he had the ball, and the referee (Mr. Renton) awarded Widnes a try in consequence. Taylor's attempt at goal just failed, the ball hitting the up- right. Widnes were penalised close in, and Poole I placed a goal for St. Helens. Just before the fin ish Taylor and Tilley scored tries, one of which was Improved by Davies. Result :—Widnes 1 goal 3 tries (11 points), St. Helens 1 goal 1 try (5 points). Teams:— _

St. Helens—Atkinson, back ; Winter, Hillen, J. Creevy, and Manchester, three-quarter backs; Toole and Bocock, half backs ; Mooney, Mavity, Pope, Smith, Dolan, and J. Prescott, forwards. Widnes—Tilley, back ; Barber, Taylor, Lambert, and Davies, three-quarter backs ; Lally and Noon, half hacks; G. Aspey, Argent, Clare, -Evans, Rigby and Turner, forwards.

div.head: RUGBY UNION.
div.p: RUGBY UNION.
STOCKTON HEATH v. NEW BRIGHTON.

, Played at New Brighton on Saturday. Stockton Heath won the toss and New Brighton from the kick off took up the attack Offside play by a visiting for- ward gave the homesters a free kick put the attempt at goal failed. New Brighton maintained the attack and a good passing, movement ended in Tomes scoring near the posts, the goal kick failing. From the drop out Stockton Heath rushed the ball to the home line a dead ball resulting. Stockton Heath continued to attack and Gerard put in a good individual run and scored for Daintith to land the goal. Half time came with the score. Stockton Heath 5 points New Brighton 3 points. For the restart Stockton Beath pressed and a good opening by Ferguson was spoiled by a had transfer. Good play by the visiting forwards kept New Brighton on the defence and from a scramble near the line Fawcett scored, Daintith fail- ing at goal. From the drop out New Brighton by good forwao play reached the visitors line but were successfully kept out. Even play followed until a mis- understanding between 'Sampson and Daintith let in Tomes who scored, a goal resulting. Final score being New Brighton 1 goal 1 try 8 points. Stockton Heath 1 goal I try S points. The Second team entertained New Brighton "B" at home and a 'rather one sided game ended in a victory for the home team by 4 goals 2 tries 26 points to nil. New Brighton were the heavier epam but the dash and com- bination of Stockton Heath nullified the visitors individual efforts. These were scored by Mclntyre (3). Hewitt (1), L. Daiutith (1), Yeomans (1), and W. Gibbs kicked 4 goals.

Baptist Church Finances. Sir,—ln reply to a letter appearing in your last issue, signed by Mr. A. P. Freeman re the Baptist Church finances we beg to say that at a church meeting held on Octoi)er 3rd 1906, it was decided to submit the church accounts to a charteesd accountant for the purpose of audit, we invite the fullest investigation, and in due course we shall make public the report of the accountant. Signed on behalC.of the church, Yours &c., H. BUCKBY. October sth, WOG.

div.head: Land Values.
div.p: Land Values.

Sir,—At tilt.) present time we are simply submerged in reforms and improvements ; but few people realise that the best reforms, the greatest improvements, in fact every progress that is made all helps in the end only to fill the pockets of the landlord, since every human pro- gress results in an increased rental value of the land. On this account reform of the land laws is the first reform which ought to be tackled, so as to stop the landlord from being thelegitimate legatee of all public improvements. A few examples will explain this need. When Sir Henry Campbell Bannerman was in charge of Woolwich Arsenal he increased the wages all round. A short time afterwards the rents in the whole town rose to an extent equal to that of the increased wages in the arsenal. The London County Council bought off the halfpenny toll over the Waterloo Bridge for .£500,000. This amounted to 6d. per week for each workman using this bridge. It was not long before the rents all around were increased by exactly the same amount 6d, which the workingman would otherwise have saved.—Anyone who takes an interest in this question ought to hear Mr. Verinder, (General Secretary of the English League for the Taxation of Land Values) speak at the Liberal Club on Thurday the 11th October at 7.30 p.m. or at the Co-operative Hall, Cairo-street on Friday the 12th at 7.30 p.m.—Yours Scc. R. OCKEL. Walton New Road, October 4th, 190 G

div.head: Rifle Shooting as a Winter Evening Pursuit.
div.p: Rifle Shooting as a Winter Evening Pursuit.

Sir,—With the approach of the autumn and winter months a problem which confronts those who are engaged during the day is "What shall we do with our winter evenings ? " and as a solution to this question I should like to again bring very forcibly to the notice of all Englishmen how incumbent it is upon them that they should become skilled in the handling of a weapon which can be used in defence of their country should ever they be called upon to defend its shores. The subject of rifle shooting has received very great prominence in the columns of the Press since the memorable warning issued to our fellow-countrymen in June of last year by the late Commander-in-Chief of the British Army, Field-Marshal Earl Roberts, and trust that I shall not be thought guilty of plagiarism if I also urge the necessity for all the young men of this country to practice rifle shooting. The Society of Miniature Rifle Clubs" of which Lord Roberts is President, and of the committee of which I am Chairman, has, during the past five years, done all in its power to make rifle shooting the pursuit and pastime of all Englishmen. Its efforts lam pleased to say have not been unsuccessful; it has been instrumental in forming over 400 rifle clubs. It has held many rifle shooting tournaments throughout the kingdom, and it has, in a word, shown how rifle shooting can he brought to the very doors of the masses. That its work is appreciated by those who are in a position to judge of its value is evidenced by the fact that the War Office has recently granted to the clubs affiliated to it the same facilities as are granted to the clubs affiliated to the National Rifle Association, prominent amongst which is exemption from payment of gun licence by members of clubs using rifle ranges for Miniature Rifle practice. I am afraid that the reason a larger number of rifle clubs do not exist at the present time is that the general public is ignorant as to the requirements necessary for the fitting up of a range, and I should like to point out that in the event of open space not being obtainable almost any hall or room of not less than say GO feet in length can at very small cost be protected in such a way as to afford facilities for the carrying on of rifle shooting practice, and if those desirous of bringing about the formation of a rifle club will communicate with the Secretary of the Society of Miniature Rifle Clubs, ;20 Bucklersbury, London, E.C., they will be
lied 'with full information on the sibject.

suPPI The cost of the erection of an indoor range is by no means great, and under ordinary circumstances a sum of £2O should more than cover the outlay necessary, and should be sufficient in addition to equip a club with at least three rifles. In conausion I should like to mention that those who are unable to themselves bring about the formation of a rifle club in any particular district can assist this great movement by a contribution, however small, towards its funds. The work that the Society of Miniature Rifle Clubs has in hand is a national one, and should receive national recognition. Our progress is greatly hampered by want of funds, and the Committee would be grateful if those interested in the society's objects would show their appreciation of its work by making a monetary contribution. I shall be very glad indeed to acknowleege any sum which may be sent to me.-1. am, sir, yours faithfully, NORFOLK, Clnirman.

Norfolk House, St. James', London, S.W. 29th September, 1906. The Right to Work Committee and the I LP. Sir,—" Gas;vorker's " somewhat hasty adieu leaving "the other points raised to some other occasion" is dis- appointing, for one of the "other points " was the burden of first letter, which practically charged the Liberal party with exploiting Trades Unions because Labour representatives are invariably found in its ranks. He has not, nor can he, controvert my assertion that these members are there as free agents either to act independently or to form a group to support or oppose any Government that may be in power, and that they support the Liberal party for the same reasons that the I present Independent Labour group is supporting the I present Liberal Ministry, i.e., because it is the most I expeditious way of securing the reforms they are seek- ing. Even Mr. Stott(whose intervention will under the circumstances be welcomed by his own party) can only offer the observation that" a large number of the mem- bers of the Miners' Federation are not satisfied with the present form of labour representation, judging from their expressed desire to join the Labour party." He does nothowever, seem to see that this is only another proof of the freedom of the Labour Members to act I apart from any Liberal party interference. Whether they act on their OWII initiative or from their Union's instruction, individually or in groups, the very nature of their wants makes them Liberals. Yet it 13 by the deliberate misrepresentation of these facts that the I.L.P. is creating its own party, fostering a spirit of bitternessiand causing division instead of unity in the ranks of the progressive forces. " Gas-worker " also leaves to" some other occasion" my request for any valid reasons why the members of the present Independent Labour section should not be classed as Liberals. Avoiding the main issue, " Gas-worker" goes on to ridicule the idea of the I.L.P. being a menace to reform when I myself admit that what is practical in their programme is part and parcel of Liberalism. Why should he thus pretend to be ignorant of the reason ? He knows as well as I do that the Liberalis:n of the LL.P. is served up adulterated with Socialism; that the practical Liberalism is made to subserve the ends of the impracticable Socialism ; that its effect is to create a cleavage in the progressive forces resulting in the build- ing up of a party whose Snowdens and Macdonalds are just as open to the charge of seeking their own material I aims and advantages as are any leaders of the Liberal

Tarty. Mr. Stott's letter is assuredly a " poser "—as regards its length. The Editor's scissors might have been use- fully applied in cacting out his " proof " that the Right to Work Committee is not a " decoy," for he simply gives the history of the formation of the committee part of which I gave myself. You can no more prove the genuineness of the committee from its history than you can determine the length of an object by measuring its breadth. Such reasoning as this seems to be a feature inherent in the Socialist .mitid. We were of course quite aware that the committeo. emanated from the Right to Work National Council which is an organisation of the usual I.L.P. concoFtien. The question is not how or when this. committee was formed but " What is its object ?" Is its object as its name implies, to secure for the people the Right to Work apart from Socialism which is the object of the I.L.P. ? It has been remarked to me that Liberalism has no remedy for the unemployed vestion but that the I.L.P. has, and this Right to Work Committee has been pointed out as the remedy. Now I should like to ask Mr. Stott to state whether it is not a fact that his party leaders frankly acknowledge that there cannot possibly be a solution of the Unemployed question until the Socialist state is realised and that they do not at present know the social order of that far off time by which Unemployment is made to be impossible ; that the proposals for dealing with Unemployment embodied in the scope of the Right to Work Committee are so many "economic makeshifts " the principles of which have been applied often enough in the past and have been found wanting. Will Mr. Stott also say whether, if this committee is not what it professes to be. it is not a deception ; and if a deception whether it may not appropriately be described as a " decoy "since its object, if a sham, can only be to attract to the I.L.P. Mr. Stott's letter is not without the usual perversions
4 '4 e. 41,1" taltVri

of sense. When he speaks of" ending "for instance it is in a different sense than the one in which I used it. If the I.L.P. were to come out into the open as the Liberals and Conservatives do there would be nothing to complain of so far as their tactics are concerned. But if our League were to resort to the methods of the I.L.P. we should send our mem- ber to their respective Unions to see that things there were carried on in the interests of the Liberal party, in which case we might have received an " invitation" to join this Right to Work Committee. If Conserva- tives took the same course it is not difficult to conjec- ture as to the intrigues that must necessarily be carried on within the Unions and this is the intriguing to which I referred. If the Unions were to be exploited in this way by the three parties, they would not last twelve months. I may also point out another misquotation. I said that some of the most extreme items of the I.L.P. programme were advocated by sections of the Liberal party. Had these questions become party measures they could have been carried through. Mr. Stott seems to have the idea that when a Government is in power it can do what it likes and so re-organise the whole of society from beginning to end. If he will only reflect he must see that a government is dependent upon the sections that support it which ought I think to impress him with the importance of directing his efforts in co-operating with other progressive parties, to make the individuals, sections or groups which support a government as progressive as possible, for the Govern- ment is bound to reflect the political sympathies of its supporters,otherwise it could not stand. I notise a perhaps not unnatural tendency on the part of Mr. Stott to wander into subjects that are not rele- vant to the question under discussion. But I should like to refer to the Right to Labour League which he has introduced, because its object is to do on an economically sound basis what the Right to Work Committee professes to do on "economic makeshifts." By the latter people are put to work in such a way that the percentage of unemployment is not permanently affected, but which has the effect of reducing the the earnings of those in regular employment, the workers themselves being buoyed up with the thought that" Socialism is coming." On the other hand, the Right to Latour League recognising that it is mainly an economic question,would put the unemployed to work in such a way that unemployment would cease and by the withdrawal of the unemployed from the labour market wages would generally rise. I can scarcely expect Mr. Stott to see9through our scheme when his thoughts are turned in thti one direction. Probably he has given little attention to it, but if he likes to take the trouble to compare the methods advocated by his committee and those advocated by the Right to Labour League, I will do my best to show him wherein his are fallacious and our's sound. As an instance of the apparent insincerity of the Socialists, I may say that I laid the scheme of the Right to Labour League before the leaders of one of our land-grabbing fraternities who are of course Socialists. They admitted that they had no remedy to suggest—were in fact simply agitating—but our scheme was too drastic and would frighten people. Whatever scheme is destined to settle the unemployed question will cause a vast change in industry, a change ' which Socialists of all people profess to desire, and yet they can be the first to be shocked. If Mr. Stott's sympathies for the submerged are stronger than his party prejudices he will consider with open mind any genuine suggestion for the solution of the, greatest modern problem.—Yours truly, JOHN MORTON, Hon. Sec. Progressive Labour League. Warrington, Sept. 4tia, 190 G.

div.head: MENIMMEIIIMa
div.p: MENIMMEIIIMa
PRETTY WEDDING AT PENKETH.
Woodward—Ambler.

The Wesleyan Church, Penketh. was the scene of a very pretty wedding on Wednesday afternoon,the con- tracting parties being Miss Winifred Edith Ambler, younger daughter of Mr. and Mrs. J. T Ambler, Ash , Cottage, Penketh, and Lieutenant Reginald Arthur ; Woodward, R.N.R., eldest son of the late Mr. George Arthur Woodward,of Liscard, Cheshire. The wedding aroused considerable interest in the village and a large congregation assembled. The Rev. John Gunnell was the officiating minister. Mr. Frank Hickman pre- sided at the organ and played appropriate selections, and the hymn The voice that breathed o'er Eden" , was sung. The bride, who was :given away by her ; father, was charmingly dressed in writ y satin,trimmed ' with tulle and guipure lace. Her veil was also of I tulle and was sui mounted with a wreath of orange blossom, and she carried a lovely bouquet of white heather and roses and lilies of the valley. The I bridesmaid was Miss Muriel Worlidge (cousin of the bride) wha wore a very pretty dress of white French embroidered muslin over pink silk and carried a ; bouquet of marguerites. Her ornament was a pearl brooch,the gift of the bridegroom. The bride's mother was tastefully gowned in green silk, with Tuscan hat, I and her bouquet was composed of pale pink roses I The bridegroom was in naval uniform. Mr. Harold Ambler, (brother of the bride) discharged the duties of best man. At the close of the ceremony a reception was held at Ash Cottage and a large number of guests were present. Later the newly-married couple left for the Channel Island's where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride's travelling dress was of tailor- made blue serge, with hat to match. div.head: NATIONAL FREE CHURCH COUNCIL'S AUTUMN
div.p: NATIONAL FREE CHURCH COUNCIL'S AUTUMN
CAMPAIGN.

Rev. Thomas Law, general Secretary of the National Council of the Evangelical Free Churches has just completed the arrangements for the Free Church Education Campaign which is to be carried out during the autumn. Most of the chief centres of England and Wales will be included. The campaign will open OD Monday, October 3th with a demonstration in the large I Drill Hall, Derby. The principal speakers then will be Dr. John Clifford and Mr. J. Compton Rickett M.P. I Plymouth will be visited by Dr. Clifford and Rev. Thomes Phillips 8.A., on October 15th. Dr. Clifford will also speak at Cardiff on November 9th with Rev. C. Silvester Horne M.A., at Newcastle-on-Tyne on November 12th with Rev. J. Hirst Hollowell,at Preston on November 13th with Rev. A. T. Guttery. These centres alone include about 120 local Councils and Federations. The whole of the 900 Councils have the matter under consideration and in many cases are making local arrangements.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, October 6, 1906.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, October 6, 1906.
THE BIRTLES PROPERTY.
TWO SIDES OF A BARGAIN DISCUSSED.
Lively Council Debate.

A. somewhat heated debate took place at the meeting of the Town Council on -Tuesday evening with refer- ence to the transaction between Mr. Thomas Birtles and the Corporation' concerning the purchase of property in Sankey-street. • On the agenda it was reported that a long discussion took place at the General Purposes Committee with regard to the assignment of land and premises in Sankey-street, from Mr. Thomas Birtles to the Corpora- tion, and it was ultimately resolved "that the meeting be adjourned." In the list of documents requiring the seal of the Corporation, however, appeared the " assignment of plot of land Sankey-street, from T. Birtles to the Corporation." Councillor LORD objected to the common seal of the Corporation being affixed to the assignment and remarked that in that connection he would like to ask the Borough Treasurer one or two questions. The 3lavon : Will that be in order ? Move an amendment that the seal be not affixed or the matter referred back. Councillor LORD : Cannot we discuss it without doing that? The Slavoß : I daresay you can ; it is on the minutes. Councillor LORD asked the Borough Treasurer I whether or not he had been approached by an estate agent of Warrington with regard to the sale of this land? The BOROUGH TREASURER: Yes, I was. Councillor LORD : Can you tell us the date you I were approached? The BOROUGH TREASURER: I cannot. I made no note of it. Councillor LORD : Well, I presume you were , approached some time prior to the actual purchase ? The Boironort TREASURER: It was before the pur- chase of course ; but it is so long ago that I cannot remember the date. Councillor LORD : What course did you pursue afterwards ? Did you negotiate the matter ? The BoßouGri TREASURER : No; I had nothing to do with the negotiations of the committee. The MAYOR : This is rather irregular. It should be dEalt with in committee. Councillor PEMBERTON : It is very important, Mr. Mayor. The MAYOR : If the Council wishes it to go on I am satisfied. Councillor WILKINsox : Let him go on ! The MAYOR: Will you (the Council) take tie res- ponsibility ? Councillor LORD : I will take the responsibility. (To the Borough Treasurer) What action did you take ? The BOROUGH TREASURER : I did what I should do is every case. I reported it to the Town Clerk. Councillor LORD : You finished there ? The BOROUGH TREASURER : I have nothing else to say. Councillor LORD: You had nothing more to do with it: The BOROUGH TREASURER: No. Councillor Loan: I understand the Borough Surveyor , was also approached on the matter. I The BOROUGH SURVEYOR : Never; not until it came before the committee. Councillor LORD: Then I should like to know what the Town Clerk did in this matter. (Laughter.) The TOWN CLERK : Negotiate for the purchase. I Councillor LORD : Who with? The TOWN CLERK: With Mr. Birtles. Councillor LORD : Not with the estate agent? The TOWN CLERK: No. Councillor LORD: Where does Mr. Birtles come in? The TOWN CLERK : What do you mean ? Councillor. LORD said he understood that the Borough Treasurer told tde Town Clerk he had been approached by the estate agent. The TOWN CLERK : That is quite true. Councillor LORD : What did you do then ? The TOWN CLERK : Saw Mr. Birtles. Councillor LORD : Why go to him? He was not the estate agent. The Tows CurtK: I did not know the estate agent. I did not see him. Councillor LORD : I presume Mr. Fairhurst told you. I want to know what the Town Clerk did with regard to being approached by the agent. The TOWN CLERK : I heard that the property was in the market, and I saw Mr. Birtles, and he said he had the option of the purchase. The MAYOR said he could vouch for that. Mr. Birtles had a letter from Mr. Robert Garnett giving him the offer of the" first refusal." Councillor LORD : I should like Mr. Fairhurst to say whether he told the Town Clerk who the estate agent was? The MAYOR : Is this another committee of inquiry? Councillor WILKINSON: Tell the estate agent's name. Tbe BOROUGH TREASURER said it was so long ago that he could not remember his conversation with the Town Clerk. He could remember that when he got off I a car in Rylands-street Mr. Robert Lowe told him that he had been asked to sell the property belonging to Mr. R. Garnett at the corner of Legh-street, and said he would like to know whether it would be of any use to the Corporation. He(Mr. Fairhurst) said he did not know, but that he would mention it to the Town Clerk. He mentioned it to Mr. Whittle—whether on the same day he did not know, but he.sapposed he should take an early opportunity. That was the only recollection he had of what took place. They must bear in mind that it happened four years ago. Councillor Loran': You told the Town Clerk that you had met Mr. Robert Lowe. The BOROUGH TREASURER : I should no doubt—l cannot say positively—tell him that Mr. Lowe was em- powered to negotiate for the sale of the property. Councillor LORD : I fail to see why the Town Clerk did not negotiate with the estate agent—and for Alder- man Tiunion's benefit I might say my inquiry is all over • Alderman TENSION : Even if it is not, I seriously object. This cross-examination is a gross mistake. Toe MAYOR : Well I asked the Council if they objected and they did not, so they take the respon- sibility. Alderman TENSION thought that for a man to ask questions in that way was a farce. Councillor LORD: I have the whole of the questions down here that I intended to ask. The MAYOR: You cam ask questions with a double meaning which deceive people who have to answer them. I can ask you questions you could not answer straight. ' Councillor PEMBERTON : Ask them. The Mayo : You know the way of asking such questions. Councillor LORD : You can ask me any question. you like to put. Continuing he said lae failed to understand why, seeing that they had the opportunity of negoti- ating direct with Mr. Garnett or his agent, those negotiations were not entered into and Mr. Birtles was approached. Councillor Lord proceeding said : This land was orginally the 'property of the late Mr. Robert Garnett, whose agent offered it direct to the Corporation in 1902. Mr. Garnett's desire to sell was communicated to Mr. Males, who then arranged with Mr. Garnett that the property should be sold to or through him. He thereupon contracted (through the Town Clerk) for the sale to the Corporation of part of this property, and for the retention by him of the other part, as set forth in an agreement dated the 29th , November 1902. The price for the whole property was I £l,OOO and it was subject to a ground rent of £43 10s. per year. Under this agreement the Corporation agreedl to lend Sir. Birtles £2,000 at 4 per cent, per annum interest till the completion of the purchase, this sum to be secured by a mortgage on the premises retained by Mr. Birtles. The .£4,000 for the full purchase from Mr. Garnett was paid on December 2nd 1902 by the Corporation, the amount for the portion retained by Mr. Birtles being £l7lB 2s. 4d. or with apportionment of stamp duty aci interest £1723 Is. Od. Under the agreement the Corporation also agreed to pay to Mr. Birtles on the completion of the purchase (it is not yet completed) for the agreed approximate cost of erecting new buildings (in place of the old buildings) the sum of £2,200 in cash ; the material of the old buildings when pulled down to remain the property of Mr. Birtles The law costs of the purchase by Mr. Birtles from Mr. Garnett, including stamp duty were, under the agreement, to be borne in Equal parts by Mr. Birtles and the Corporation. In respect of the above arrange- ments the Corporation has paid £8,594 Os. 3d. as below : s. d. Dec. 2nd 1902 By Robert Garnett 4,000 0 0 By Stamp Duty and interest 22 15 3 By Birtles (to build and rebuild) as below On March 25th 1901 l7O 0 0 April 22nd „ June 14th „ Oct. 19th 50 0 0 April 19th 1905 250 0 9 May 2nd „ Juee 9th „ June 28th „ Aug. 9th ~ Sept. 21st „ Oct. 31st ~

(2nd) that the Corporation is to reoeive from Mr. Birties for his proportion of the original purchase £1,728 is. 9d. and (3rd) that the parts of the properties retained by the Corporation have cost the Corporation £4,404 13s. ed. It would be interesting to note what the Corporation has got for this large amount of £4,494 13s. Gd. but the immediate question is the result to Mr. Birtles of the deal. He has got :

No estimate has been made of the value to Mr. Birtles of his improved position, nor of the enhanced value of the land. According to the assignment of 29th November, 1902, Mr. Birtles was not to receive any part of the £2,200 for the building purposes till the completion of the purchase. It will be seen that he has received all this sum, and 6 further advance, before the completion of the purchase. Also although the Corporation were to be secured by a mortgage on the premises, there was a considerable interval during which there was little to secure the mortgage. And, further that whereas Mr. Birtles was to have paid a moiety of the stamp charges on the purchase from Mr. Garnett, he has only been debited with a proportion thereof. I will have to move that this matter be sent back for further enquiry. Whoever had charge of it the interests of the Corporation were not considered and they struck a very bad bargain. The MAYOR : It is signed, sealed and settled. Councillor PEMBERTON : No. It is not. The MAYOR: I understand it is. Councillor PEMBERTON : It has not passed the Council.

Councillor ASHCROFT : After the remarks by Mr. Fairhurst I think the matter ought to go back and I second the amendment. Councillor MaGINN said if he was in Mr. Birtles' position he would make the Corporation go to arbitra- tion for the property. They were told by Councillor Lord that Mr. Birtles had made a fabulous fortune out of the property. The strangest thing was that Garnett's allowed such a good bargain to go into Mr. Birtles' hands and allowed him to make such a fortune. He thought that if anyone had made a bad bargain it had been Mr. Birtles. Mr. CRAIK asked if anyone knew whether Mr. Robert Lowe was an accredited agent for Mr. Garnett. The MAYOR : If Mr. Lowe saw a good bargain he would not let it slip. Mr. CRAIK : If he was not the accredited agent for Mr. Garnett we have no right to take him into the question at all. Councillor WrLKINsON : It does not matter whether an estate agent approached the Borough Treasurer as it is a fact that Mr. Birtles had tbo option of the property from Mr. Garnett. I have seen the letter which Mr. Garnett wrote. It is deplorable when private correspondence between two such re.ipectablo families has to be dragged up here for purposes which he all know. As a matter of fact Mr. Garnett was approached and offered more for the property but he said Mr. Birtles had been a good tenant and should have it. When Mr. Birtles got the offer of the land for £4,000 from Mr. Garnett he asked the Corporation to finance him. Man honourable man he approached the Property Purchasing Committee who were equally honourable

men. Councillor PEMBERTON : You are one. Councillor WILKINSON : I ask Councillor Pemberton for once in his life to endeavour to be a gentleman. Councillor PE3ILSI:TON : Don't praise yourself. No gentleman would. Councillor %WILKINSON continuing, said that as business men the Committee saw a good bargain for ' the Corporttion, agreed to find Mr.Birtles £4OO and the bargain was closed and the Corporation took half the estate. They had quite sufficient for their £2,000, and he claimed that the mortgage was well secured. In fact on the security anyone would have financed Mr. Birtles. 'Mr. Birtles had always paid the account when it was ready with interest, and if he had not had a friend in the Corporation he would have had a few friends in Warrington who would have taken him up. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Birtles had the option, and that set aside the possibility of anyone else coming in. He was proud to say that Mr. Birtles had made something out of the matter, but it had been made on his investment. The Corporation had only been his financiers, they had only financed him with £2,000 which any bank or solicitor would have done, and what had the Corporation got ? one half of the road, and one of the best sites in War- rington,for which otherwise they had would have to pay £7 10s.a yard,or between £3,000 and £4,ooo.There had been no underhand work, and the Town Clerk had only one object from beginning to end—the serving of the interests of Warrington. The MAYOR said they had one side put by Councillor Lord, but no one seemed to have an idea what a bargain the Corporation had got. The Corporation had not lost a single fathing by the transaction, which was one that would bring in a revenue instead of being a cost to the ratepayers. (Hear, hear.) His Worship then read the following printed statement with reference to the position of Mr. Birtles and the Corporation The following figures show the final effect of the transaction between Mr. T. Birtles and the Corporation. It will be seen that the figures differ somewhat from those given to the General Purposes Committee, this being brought about by the inclusion of additional ratable tenements. £ s. d. The rates which the Corporation received before the improvement (including water, poor, improvement, and sewers) amounted to The rates which will be payable on the increased ratable value amount to - Or an annual increase of The property and improvement has cost the Corporation t£4,491 13s. 6(1., which must be repaid in 60 years. Interest and sinking fund represents £lBl 0 0 Add to this the ground rent payable by Corporation
.£204 10 4 From this must be deducted— Rent of education offices Rent of land leased to the Motor Co. 90 0 0

Alderman BENNETT said he believed the Corporation had made a good bargain, in fact he did not see that they could have made a better bargain. He did not believe Mr. Garnett would have been disposed to offer the property to the Corporation at the same price he would offer it to Mr. Birtles, considering the old friendship between them,and Mr.Birtles had practically given the Corporation the same terms. They had therefore, reason to be thankful. At the last meeting of the Council he said his friends were • con- tinually finding mare's nests and whether he was right or wrong in all cases he certainly thought that the matter under discussion was a mare's nest. He had seen the letter to Mr. Birtles and Mr. Garnett undoubtedly gave him the option of the property, and in face of that he thought they would have been extremely ill- advised not to have closed the bargain. They had done their best for the ratepayers. Councillor PEMBERTON : The ratepayers are very much against this. Councillor WILKINSON: Bosh

Councillor PEMBERTON said all this discussion only showed how careless Alderman Bennett and some members were. They did not take the trouble to verify statements. The printed statement which the Mayor had read was ridiculous. Was any member of the Cor- poration so unbusiness-like as to dream that all the rates they got were absolute profit ? Did the Town •Clerk, the Deputy Town Clerk, and the scavengers and all the bag of tricks work for nothing ? It was ridicu- lous to say it was all absolute profit. (Hear, hear.) The paper which had been read contained the most ridicu- lous proposition. The increased ratable value only showed the value the Corporation had missed. The auditors had twice reported upon this transaction as being not altogether in order. Councillor WILKINSON : As being incomplete. The Maxon : Let him ramble about. _

&Tine-in-or WILKINSON: We want no side issues. Connelllor PEMBERTON continuing, said he declared distinctly and deliberately that it was not true that Mr. Birtles had the option in the matter. He spoke highly of Mr. Lowe, and said he would take his word as soon as anyone else's. Councillor WILKINSON : There is not a member of the council who has said one word against Mr. Lowe. (Hear, hear.) Councillor PEMBERTON : It has been suggested that Mr. Lowe came and offered the property on his own. Continuing, he said Mr. Garnett employed an agent who went directly to Mr. Fairhurst. After that Mr. Birtles went and saw Mr. Garnett. Why did not the Corpora- tion enter into the negotiations immediately after Mr. Lowe's offer. He had no feeling against Mr. Birtles, who was an old and honoured tradesman, but he objected to private arrangements being made by officials which were not in the interests of the Corporation. The property had cost the Corporation more like £6,400, and he said they ought to have seized the opportunity of buying it when first offered. The matter had never had the consent of the Council, and he was astonished that the members should sit there like so many dummies and allow such things to be passed. Councillor WRIGHT: We are as wide awake as you. If there are any dummies it is the voting machine around you. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Councillor Dr. JosEert : I will corroborate that. Continuing, Dr. Joseph said that Councillor Pemberton always seemed to insinuate that no one knew anything but himself, and that had turned,,him against almost everything he said. He had had some experience in business matters, and he did not see that he should be treated as if he were a boy. There were two points to consider—had Mr. Birtles the option and had he made a profit? The case as put by Councillor Wilkinson and others seemed to be unanswerable, and he should there- fore vote accordingly. Councillor STOTT : Messrs. Birtles and Garnett have made a good thing out of the transaction and I would like to kno7 at whose expense ? Continuing he said that certain statements had been made that the Corpor- ation had the option of purchasing the property before Mr. Birtles. . .

ICouncillo. Witt: itlsoN : We never had the option. The MAYOR : You may take it for granted that the Corporation never had the option. , Councillor STOTT said the two statements conflicted. If the Corporation had the first option a had bargain had been made. If it was true that Mr. Birtles had the option the Corporation had done very well indeed. The question was whether it would have been possible to have made a better bargain. It was is shame and a scandal in an intelligent community that it should be I possible for an individual to make an increased profit from year to year from the increased value of land when that land had been given a value by the ratepayers. Alderman SMETHURST pointed out that Mr. Birtles and the late Mr. Garnett had been bosom friends for 40 or 50 years and there was atacit understanding between them that if Mr. Birtles wanted the property he should ; have it for old friendship's sato.

div.head: Mk. BIRTLES INTERVIEWED.
div.p: Mk. BIRTLES INTERVIEWED.
"EVERYTHING STRAIGHT AND ABOVE-BOARD."

With the object of ascertaining the views of the 7entlemon most concerned in the transaction our representative on Thursday waited upon Jr. Thomas Birtles, who very readily consented to give his version of the matter which has been the cause of so much discussion.

There had, he said, for many years been an under- standing between the late Mr. Robert Garnett, and himself as old friends, that if ever the property had to be sold he (Mr. Birtles) should have the first option of purchasing it. In September, 1902, Mr. Birtles was informed that a local company was negotiating for the purchase of the building I now occupied as the Borough Education offices. He immediately went to see Mr. Garnett at the offices of the firm and reminded him of the understanding between them as to the property and asked him if he was disposed to sell. Mr. Garnett intimated his willingness to let Mr. Birtles have the property for .4:,4,000, and also said he would allow him time to consider it. Mr. Birtles went home and the same night he wrote to Mr. Garnett stating that he was prepared Ito purchase at the price named. Early the following morning (September 27th) he went to Penketh and when he reached the gate of Hall Nook, Mr. Garnett's residence, the coachman handed him a letter from Mr. Garnett which he was about to bring t.) him. Our representative saw this communication which stated : "I have your letter. I think you have done a wise thing. There is money in it. It would be wise to have a temporary agreement, as things are so uncertain." The last sentence is explained by the fact that at that time Mr. Garnett was in a very delicate state of health. The arrangement to purchase was concluded that morning and Mr. Birtles paid% a deposit of .+:5O Before he approached the Town Cl•erk, Mr. Birtles , informed our reporter, he had an interview with an influential gentleman whom he asked to finance him I and he had documentary evidence to prove that these negotiations took place before he went near the Town Clerk. The property came in hi% (Mr. Dirties') I possession before ever the matter of the Corporation acquiring some of it was broached. 1 Hearing that the Sankey-street proprty was scheduled for improvements, continued Mr. Birtles, be went to the Town Clerk and told him that he had purchased the property. If the Corporation would I advance him the money, he said, he would sell them the Education office and the front land at the price he .had paid for them—without any profit. If,howevcr, the 'committee could see their way to allow him anything en the purchase he would be very glad. " Then the purchase from r.Garnett was arranged before the Town Clerk had anything to do with the matter ?" asked the interviewer. Mr. Birtles replied emphatically in the affirmative. " Mr. Whittle never came into my place and I never went to him till tit e whole purchase was settled."

Mr. Billies added t.hat -before he approached the Corporation it had become a matter of general know- ledge that he had acquired the property. To continue the story of the negotiations, Mr. Birtles bought the property from Mr. Garnett for £4,000 and the Corporation took one half at about £2,ooo—the same price, said Mr. Bin.les, that he paid for it. •

Mr. Birtles obtained a valuation of the front land, which our representative was plivileged to inspect, and this placed a figure of .€."7 10s. per yard on the plot. The price which Mr. Thirties actually obtained from the Corporation was a little over .£2 per yard. The Corporation advanced Mr. Dirties the purchase

money at 4 per cent—which interest was paid each half year. Mr. Birtles informed our representative that a few months ago he intimated his willingness to take the property back from the Corporation and to refund the money. He also had an offer for the Education Offices from a private individual. As recently as last week he offered to appear before the committee and give a full explanation of his position in regard to the transaction but the committee apparently did not consider this course necessary.
" Everything has been straight and above-board " concluded Mr. Birtles. " There is no hole-and-corner work about this and the innuendoes cast at Mr. Whittle are simply abominable."

div.head: Estate Agent's Position.
div.p: The Estate Agent's Position.

Interviewed by an " Examiner " reporter yesterday the estate agent mentioned in connection with the transaction spoke with some reluctance as Ile had no desire whatever to be antagonistic to Mr. Birtles or anyone else. He, however, definitely assured our representative that when he approached Mr. Fair- hurst about four years ago he was acting as the accredited agent of the late Mr. Robert G-arnett and on that gentleman's personal instructions. No mention of an option in favour of Mr. Birtles had been made to him.

A private company had previously made applica- tion for the property, but the agent suggested that as the property would in all probability be required for street improvements it should first be submitted to the Corporation. Mr. Garnett thereupon instructed him to offer the property to the Corporation. A few days after seeing Mr. Fairhurst, the agent further stated, he mentioned the matter to Mr. Longdin, the Borough Surveyor, who said he would bring it before the committee.
The agent added that he had had nothing to do with the matter being brought forward at this stage

div.head: Non-Traders' Contention. To TIIE EDITOR, "EXAMINER."
div.p: The Non-Traders' Contention. To TIIE EDITOR, "EXAMINER."

Si want the ratepayers to clearlfrealise what the contention of the Non-traders is. It is. that this property, having been first offered by the late Mr. Rokiert Garnett, through his agent, direct to the Cor- poration, ought to have been accepted by the Town Clerk, who had no right to bring in Mr. Birtles, who was not the owner. We hold that as a result of this unfortunate action of the Town Clerk, the ratepayers have had to unnecessarily pay to 11r.Birtles £2,571 ss. We also contend that when, after the purchase, it became necessary to disturb Mr. Birtles, he could have been reinstated for one third of the above cost. We also join issue with the statement handed round to the members of the Council by an official on Tuesday last. We have gone into the figures of the statement most carefully, and find that instead Of the burgesses benefiting in rates to the extent of £lO a year by the deal with Mr. Birtles, they will be worse off in this respect by £O5 a year, a difference of £75 a year as compared with the figures officially given, the accuracy of which we hereby publicly challenge. For any official to be allowed, without the sanction of the Council or any Committee, to produce so altogether misleading a statement, just before an important dis- cussion, in regard to the subject covered by the statement, is most reprehensible, and that the majority of the Council should have been thereby misled is most deplorable.
Yours &c., JOHN LORD.
October sth.

div.head: BOARD OF GUARDIANS. Roman Catholic— Services at the Workhouse.
div.p: BOARD OF GUARDIANS. Roman Catholic— Services at the Workhouse.

A meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held on Wednesday under the presidency of Mr. J. Billinge. There were also present :—Mrs. Clay, Mrs. Wilkinson, Miss Broadbent, Messrs. W. Hickman, A. J. Jolley, R. Forshavv, W. C. Brooks,A. Brooks, It. Bolton, J. Payton, S. Davies, G. Mather, W. Houghton, J.Back- house, W. Flannagan, J. Cook, M. W. Seton, J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), J. F. Awbery (master), and A. Wright (superintendent of Padgate schools).

div.head: ROMAN CATHOLIC SERVICES.
div.p: ROMAN CATHOLIC SERVICES.

At a meeting of -t-he-ifOiise—.CO;;;ittee held on September 21st, Father RYAN attended and stated his views concerning the annoyances and objectionable features in connection with Catholic inmates attending his church on Sunday mornings, and suggesting that' arrangements should be made for the services to be held in the House. The committee gave the whole subject most careful consideration and after discussion it was agreed to recommend the Board to pay Father Ryan £5O a year in recognition of his undertaking to conduct services in the Workhouse and thus cease the practice of the inmates going out. The MASTER submitted a report which had been prepared by the Superintendent Nurse and having regard to the fact that the Infirmary would now be a recognized training school, it was resolved to sanction four probationer nurses remaining an additional year in the service of the Guardians at the rate of £2O yearly and uniform, as was now paid to the three years' pro- bationers, the future salaries to be paid to probationers to be at the following rates :—First year, £9 ; second £l2 • and third year, £l5. The committee recommend at the end of each year's course of training of the pro- bationers,an examination be held by some medical man other than the resident medical officer or the deputy. • Mr. FORSHAW moved the confirmation of the minutes. Several members of the House Committee, he said, were not satisfied with the decision as to Father Ryan as they felt the whole question of religious services for every denomination should be gone into. Mr. JOLLEY seconded.

Mr. litctimAN moved that the resolution with refer- ence to the Roman Catholic services be referred back. Many members of the House Committee were away at the Poor Law Conference when the matter was decided. The present working of the institution ought not to be interfered with any more than they could possibly help because there would be a new Board in the course of a few months.

Mr. JOLLEY contended that apart from any other question the change would be a distinct gain to the , administration of the institution and beneflcal to all I concerned. It would be welcomed by their officers and, he thought, by the House Committee. The only differ- ence of opinion was as to the amount of remuneration. 1 Some members thought the amount proposed was ! scarcely adequate for the services to he rendered. At Prescot similar services were conducted and the Roman Catholic priest received £lOO a year. Father Ryan suggested that 30s. a week would barely meet the additional expense he would have have to incur in con- nection with his church. After a friendly conversion, however, he expressed his willingness to accept £5O a year. Ho (Mr. Jolley) felt strongly that the charge would be another important improvement and reform. Mr. MATHER thought the matter had been rather hastily arranged, considering the small attendance at the committee meeting and the vagueness of the notice received. He hoped the Roman Catholics would receive religious instruction but he objected to the way in which they were spending money on the institution. He believed that during the present year they had raised wages and salaries to the tune of nearly £1 a day. In reply to Mr. Hickman, the CH AIRM AN said that there were in the institution 207 members of the Church of England, 106 Roman Catholics, 22 Nonconformists. The CHAIRMAN supported the proposal as a measure of justice. Their expenditure, he admitted, was great, but if they had efficiency they were fully compensated. Mr. PAYTON asked who looked after the Noncon- formist inmates ? The eHAIRMAN : The Nonconformists have a service on Tuesday evenings conducted by Free Church la?nen. Mr. PAYTON : If there are any other increa.s.l43 of salary I think the Nonconformists will be corning too. Why should not they be looked after as well ak the others,
On a vote being taken the amendment was defeated, and the minutes were confirmed.

DR. BRAME'S GRATUITY. - The following motions were adopted unanimously "That Dr. &aide having, at the request of the ' Guordians, resigned his office of Workhouse Medical Officer with a view to the appointment of a Resident Workhouse Medical Officer and daving claimed to be I paid, out of the common fund of the Union, a sum equal Ito the amount of all his contributions, in respect of such office, to the superannuation fund, it is resolved to pay to him the amount thereof." "That a grant to Dr. Braide, with the sanction of the Local Government Board, of a gratuity payable out of the common fund of the Union, of a sum equal to twice the amount of I:4s salary of £l5O and of his emoluments during the year,lending on the quarter day preceding the day on which he ceased to hold his office cf Work- house Medical Officer be made and paid to him upon receipt of such sanction."

IDuring the present year, says Mr. G. Mather, the Board of Guardians have raised wages and salaries to the tune of nearly ..-C1 a day ! * * * It is probably not generally known that there are more people within thirty-five miles of Manchester Exchange than within thirty-five miles of Charing Cross. South Lancashire is one of the busiest and most conjested spots on the face of the globe. The Town Council sat for three hours and a half on Tuesday. A large proportion of the time was spent in" backbiting" and the discussion of side issues. If the Mayor would resolutely put down the constant interruptions which speakers have to endure, and keep them to the point, there would be a better feeling all round and a much more expeditious dispatch of business. *s* 11 We are pleased to notice that the Rural District Council is, perhaps unconsciously, following in the steps of the Beautiful Warrington Society. Some new bye-laws have been adopted and one very sensible regulation is that in future an open space must be provided in front of all buildings which are erected. This will naturally encourage the cultivation of gardens and consequent beautification of the district. * * The claims for a lodger's vote are not often so thin as those advanced at Stalybridge on Monday. The applicant said that neither his father nor his mother had a right to certain enter rooms without his per- mission. His was the only sitting-room in the house. —The Barrister : Do you mean to say you shut the door in your mother's face ? Have your mother and father to stand on the mat and say" Please, John, can we come in ?" (Laughter.)` These claims are altogether too thin. I disallow the vote.

NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. RUGBY FOOTBALL. [By " Ovalist."] The Fates did not decree that Warrington were to g) through the present season undefeated, and I doubt whether the nlost enthusiastic follower of the club expected as much. Saturday's visit to Broughton brought the first reverse. Something of the sort was anticipated when it was learnt that three such valuable players as Isherwood, Hockenhall and Naylor were absent for various reasons. 'This practically broke the backbone of the team and in consequence they made nothing like so formidable a show at Wheater's Field as Was expected. Still they were not badly beaten, and the line was only crossed once. Eight of the Rangers' eleven points came from goals placed by the expert foot of W. Harris. In fact the latter had the distinction of getting the try also, so that he fined the bill pretty completsly. Warrington escaped being nilled, and that was all.

The War Memorial. A meeting of the War Memorial Committee was held on Monday evening, in the Drill Hall, under the presidency of Mr. Henry Roberts, to make arrange- ments for the unveiling of the statue to the late Colonel O'Leary and officers and men of the South Lancashire Regiment who fell while engaged in the South African war. There was a large attendance. It was decided that the following inscription be placed in one of the panels : To the memory of Lieutenant- Colonel W. MacCarthy O'Leary and .the officers, non- commissioned officers and men of the Prince of Wales's Volunteers (South Lancashire Regiment), who gave their lives for their country during the war in South Africa, 1899-1902. "In action faithful and in honour clear." Erected by their fellow citizens, and comrades in the Regiment. —Another panel will contain the names of the soldiers who died during the war, while a third erne will record the engage- ments in which the regiment has taken part. No date has been fi..ted for the unveiling but it is not likely to take place before the end of November. An effort is being made to prevail upon H.R.H. the Prince of Wales to perform the ceremony.
